units.la: 7. By stirring up some particular Passions, which in Opinions do usually more influence the Understanding. And here I shall only insist upon these two, Pride, and Anger; with the peculiar means that Satan hath to engage them in his Service.
units.tr: 7. By stirring up some particular passions, which in opinions usually have more influence on the understanding. Here I shall insist on only two: pride and anger, together with the particular means Satan has of enlisting them in his service.

units.la: That Pride and Anger are the two usual Firebrands of Contention, and Fountains of Error, all Ages have acknowledged and bewailed. These two Companions in Evil do so darken the Mind, that the miserable Captive, in whom they domineer, is carryed blindfold he knows not whither, nor how. Pride usually begins, and Anger follows with all its forces to justify what Pride hath undertaken. Hence the Apostle in 1 Tim. 6. 4. rakes up all the concomitant Filth of Error, as Envy, Strife, Railings, evil Surmisings, and perverse Disputings of Men, and lays them at the Door of Pride; He is proud, knowing nothing.
units.tr: All ages have acknowledged and lamented that pride and anger are the two usual firebrands of contention and fountains of error. These two companions in evil so darken the mind that the wretched captive in whom they rule is carried blindfold, not knowing where or how. Pride usually begins, and anger follows with all its force to justify what pride has undertaken. Hence the Apostle, in 1 Tim. 6. 4., gathers up all the filth that goes with error, namely envy, strife, railings, evil surmisings and perverse disputings of men, and lays them at the door of pride: He is proud, knowing nothing.

units.la: After the same manner doth the Devil engage Anger in all Disputes and Controversies, for it keeps company with Pride, wherever there is a Provocation. And besides this, Anger stirring up Injuries and Wrongs, hath often engaged Men (as it were in revenge) to change their Opinion, and to take up another Way or Doctrine. Nay often that simple Mixture of Pride and Anger which we call Emulation, hath privately tainted the Integrity of Mind, and prepared it for the next fair opportunity of Error. This is noted of Arrius, by Theodoret, that when Alexander was chosen Bishop of Alexandria, he envied him the preferency, and from thence sought occasions of Contention, which after a little while the Devil brought to his hand, as we have heard.
units.tr: In the same manner the devil engages anger in all disputes and controversies, for it keeps company with pride wherever there is provocation. Besides this, anger, stirring up injuries and wrongs, has often led men (as it were in revenge) to change their opinion and take up another way or doctrine. Indeed, that simple mixture of pride and anger which we call emulation has often quietly tainted the integrity of the mind and prepared it for the next fair opportunity of error. Theodoret notes this of Arius: when Alexander was chosen Bishop of Alexandria, Arius envied him the preferment, and from then on sought occasions of contention, which, as we have heard, the devil soon put into his hand.

units.la: So great is the power of these two Passions over the Understanding, that we have cause to wonder at their success: seldom or never can it be shown that any Ring-leader in Error was not visibly tainted with Pride, or not apparently sowred with Discontents and Emulation.
units.tr: So great is the power of these two passions over the understanding that we have cause to wonder at their success. Seldom or never can it be shown that any ringleader in error was not visibly tainted with pride, or not plainly soured by discontent and emulation.

units.la: 8. To these ways of blinding the Understanding by the Affections, I shall add but one more, which is this: Satan endeavours mainly to adorn an Errour with Truths clothing; he takes its Ornaments and Jewels to dress up a false Doctrine, that it may look more lovely and dutiful; I mean, that he designs (where Errours are capable of such an imitation) to put them into the way, method, garb and manner which Truth doth naturally use: If Truth be adorned with Zeal, Order, Strictness, or have advantageous ways of managing it self, Errour must straight-way imitate it in all these things; and though he that looks near, may easily discern that 'tis not the natural complexion of Errour, but an artificial varnish, and such as doth no more become it than a Court-dress doth become a course, clownish Country Person, (for you may at first look usually discover the Wolf under Sheeps clothing, and under the garb of the Apostles of Christ you may see the Ministers of Satan) yet are the credulous usually affected with these appearances; if they find a professed strictness, a seeming severity, an imitation of the ways of Truth, or of the fruits thereof, they commonly seek no further, but judg that to be Truth which doth the things that Truth doth; and if Errour can handsomly stand in competition with Truth, upon a pretence of being as effectual in good works, and doing things of themselves lovely, and of good report, it doth much gain upon the good liking of those whose consideration leads them not much further than fair appearances. I shall only exemplify this by the Art and policy which Julian used to set up Paganism, and to ruine Christianity, (and those who have observed the ways which he took to gain his end, will readily acknowledg he was as well skill'd in advancing Errour and suppressing Truth as any whosoever, and knew exactly to suit his designs to Mens inclinations) he observing that Christian Religion had some particular things in its practice and way, which made it's face to shine, as that it had Persons solemnly set apart by Ordination for teaching the Mysteries of the Gospel, and for managing the publick Worship of God; that these Persons were to be grave in their carriage, and exemplary in a strict holy conversation; that the Constitutions of Religion appointed certain necessary and effectual ways of Discipline, for Punishment, and restoring of Offenders, and bringing them to Repentance; that it took care of the comfortable maintenance of those that had given up themselves to the Ministry of the Word and Prayer; that it also enjoyed a relief of the Poor and Strangers, &c. Taking notice (I say) of these Excellencies in Christianity, and how lovely they were in the eyes of their enemies; He appointed the like Constitutions for Paganism, and ordained that the Idol Temples should be suited in conveniency and comliness to Christian Churches; That there should be Seats and Desks for the chief Doctors and Readers of Gentilism, who at set-times were to exhort the People, and pray with them; and that Colledges and Monasteries should be erected for them, and for the relief of the Poor and Strangers; he commanded Discipline and Penances for the chastisement of Offenders; he required that their Priests should seriously give up themselves to the Worship of God, as also their Families; that they should not frequent Shews and Taverns, nor practise any infamous Trade and Art. Thus Sozomen reports him, and gives us a Copy of his Letter to Arsacius high Priest of Galatia to this purpose; and all this he did to bring Gentilism into credit with the Vulgar, whom he had observed to be affected to Christianity for its Order, Strictness and Government.
units.tr: 8. To these ways of blinding the Understanding through the Affections I shall add only one more. Satan labours chiefly to adorn an error with the clothing of Truth: he takes the ornaments and jewels of Truth to dress up a false doctrine, so that it may look more lovely and dutiful. That is, where errors are capable of such an imitation, he sets them in the way, method, garb and manner which Truth naturally uses. If Truth is adorned with zeal, order, strictness, or has advantageous ways of managing itself, Error must straightway imitate it in all these things. Though one who looks closely may easily discern that this is not the natural complexion of Error but an artificial varnish, which suits it no more than a courtly dress suits a rough, clownish countryman (for at first sight one may usually discover the wolf under sheep's clothing, and under the garb of the apostles of Christ one may see the ministers of Satan), yet the credulous are usually taken in by these appearances. If they find a professed strictness, a seeming severity, an imitation of the ways of Truth or of its fruits, they commonly seek no further, but judge that to be Truth which does the things Truth does. And if Error can hold its own against Truth, pleading that it is as effective in good works, and in doing things that are in themselves lovely and of good report, it gains much in the good opinion of those whose consideration does not lead them much beyond fair appearances. I shall illustrate this only by the art and policy which Julian used to set up paganism and to ruin Christianity. (Those who have observed the ways he took to gain his end will readily acknowledge that he was as skilled in advancing error and suppressing truth as anyone, and knew exactly how to suit his designs to men's inclinations.) He observed that the Christian religion had certain features in its practice and manner which made its face shine: that it had persons solemnly set apart by ordination for teaching the mysteries of the Gospel and for conducting the public worship of God; that these persons were to be grave in their bearing and exemplary in a strict, holy conduct; that the constitutions of the religion appointed certain necessary and effective ways of discipline, for punishing and restoring offenders and bringing them to repentance; that it took care for the comfortable maintenance of those who had given themselves to the ministry of the Word and prayer; and that it also provided relief for the poor and strangers, and so on. Noting (I say) these excellences of Christianity, and how lovely they appeared in the eyes of its enemies, he appointed the like constitutions for paganism. He ordained that the idol temples should be fitted in convenience and seemliness to Christian churches; that there should be seats and desks for the chief teachers and readers of heathenism, who at set times were to exhort the people and pray with them; and that colleges and monasteries should be founded for them, and for the relief of the poor and strangers. He commanded discipline and penances for the chastising of offenders; he required that their priests should seriously devote themselves, and their families, to the worship of God; and that they should not frequent shows and taverns, nor practise any infamous trade or art. Thus Sozomen reports him, and gives us a copy of his letter to Arsacius, high priest of Galatia, to this effect. And he did all this to bring paganism into credit with the common people, whom he had observed to be attached to Christianity for its order, strictness and government.

units.la: Yet is not this the only instance that may be given in this kind: for observe but any Errour that by Schism sets up for it self in a distinct party, and you shall see that though it departs from the Truth of the Church, and from its Communion, yet still (as the Israelites did with the Egyptians) it carries away with it these Jewels of the Church, and keeps to some considerable part of the Churches way, (though modified according to its own bent) that it might have a lustre with it, to make it taking with others.
units.tr: Nor is this the only instance of its kind that may be given. For observe any error that by schism sets itself up in a distinct party, and you will see that, although it departs from the truth of the Church and from its communion, yet still (as the Israelites did with the Egyptians) it carries away with it these jewels of the Church, and keeps to some considerable part of the Church's way (though modified according to its own bent), so that it may have a lustre about it, to make it attractive to others.

units.la: These eight particulars are the most remarkable ways of Satan, whereby the Affections are gained to a good liking of Errour, and by them the judgment secondarily corrupted to call it Truth.
units.tr: These eight particulars are the most remarkable ways of Satan by which the affections are won over to a favourable liking of error, and by them the judgment is secondarily corrupted to call it truth.

units.la: Satan's Attempts against the Peace of God's Children, evidenced, (1.) By his Malice; (2.) From the concernment of Peace to God's Children. What these Concerns are, explained. (3.) From the Advantages which he hath against them by disquieting their Minds.
units.tr: Satan's attempts against the peace of God's children, shown (1.) by his malice; (2.) from the importance of peace to God's children, what these concerns are being explained; (3.) from the advantages which he has against them by disturbing their minds.

units.la: 1. Confusion of Mind. 2. Unfitness for Duty, and how. 3. Rejection of Duty. 4. A stumbling-block to others. 5. Preparation of the Mind to entertain venemous Impressions, and what they are. 6. Bodily Weakness. 7. Our Miseries Satan's contentment.
units.tr: 1. Confusion of mind. 2. Unfitness for duty, and how. 3. Rejection of duty. 4. A stumbling-block to others. 5. Preparation of the mind to receive venomous impressions, and what these are. 6. Bodily weakness. 7. Our miseries are Satan's contentment.

units.la: WE have viewed the ways of Satan by which he tempts to Sin, by which he withdraws Men from Duty and Service, by which he corrupts the Mind through Errour; it only now remains that something be spoken of his attempts against the Peace and Comfort of the Children of God.
units.tr: We have looked at the ways of Satan by which he tempts to Sin, by which he draws men away from Duty and Service, and by which he corrupts the Mind through Error. It remains only to speak of his attempts against the Peace and Comfort of the Children of God.

units.la: That 'tis also one of Satans chief designs to cheat us of our Spiritual Peace, may be fully evinced by a consideration of his Malice, the great concern of inward Comfort to us, and the many Advantages which he hath against us by the disquiet of our Minds.
units.tr: That it is also one of Satan's chief designs to cheat us of our spiritual peace may be fully shown by considering his Malice, the great concern we have in inward comfort, and the many advantages which he gains against us by the disquiet of our minds.

units.la: First, Whosoever shall seriously consider the Devil's implacable Malice, will easily believe, that he so envies our Happiness that he will industriously rise up against all our Comforts. 'Tis his inward fret and indignation that Man hath any interest in that Happiness from which he irrecoverably fell, and that the Spirit of God should produce in the hearts of his People any spiritual joy or satisfaction in the belief and expectation of that Felicity, and therefore must it be expected that his Malice (heightned by the torment of his own guilt, which (as some think) are those Chains of darkness in which he is reserved at present, to the judgment of the great day) will not, cannot leave this part of our Happinefs unattempted. He endeavours to fupplant us of our Birthright, of our Bleffing, of our Salvation, and the comfortable hopes thereof. From his common imployment in this matter,the Scripture hath given him names, importing an oppofition to Chrift and his Spirit, in the ways they take for our Comfort and Satisfaction. Chrift is our Advocate that pleads for us, Satan is Διάβολος[?], a Calumniator. The Spirit interceds for us, Satan is Κατήγορος[?] τῶν ἀδελφῶν, the Accuser of the Brethren, who accuseth them before God night and day. The Spirit is our Comforter, Satan is our Disturber, a Beelzebub who is ever raking in our Wounds, as Flyes upon Sores. The Apostle Paul had his Eye upon this, when he was advising the Corinthians to receive again the penitent incestuous Person, his caution was most serious, 2 Cor. 2. 11. lest Satan get advantage of us, lest he deceive and circumvent us, (for his expression relates to Men, cunningly deceitful in Trade, that do over-reach and defraud the unskilful): and the reason of this caution was, the known and commonly experienced subtilty of Satan, for we are not ignorant of his devices, implying that he will, and frequently doth ly at catch to take all advantages against us. Some indeed restrain these advantages to Verf. 10. as if Paul only meant, that Satan was designing to fix the Corinthians upon an Opinion, that Backsliders into great Sins were not to be received again, or that he laid in wait to raise a Schism in the Church upon the account of this Corinthian. Others restrain this advantage which he waited for, to Verf. 7. where the Apostle expresseth his fear, lest the excommunicated Person should be swallowed up of too much sorrow; but the caution being not expresly bound up to any one of these, seems to point at them all, and to tell us that Satan drives on many designs at once, and that in this Mans case Satan would endeavour to put the Corinthians upon a Pharisaical rigour, or to rend the Church by a division about him, and to oppress the Penitent by bereaving him of his due comfort; so that it appears still, that it is one of his designs to hinder the Comfort, and molest the Hearts of God's Children.
units.tr: First, whoever seriously considers the Devil's implacable Malice will easily believe that he so envies our happiness that he will busily rise up against all our comforts. It is his inward gnawing and indignation that man should have any share in that happiness from which he fell beyond recovery, and that the Spirit of God should produce in the hearts of his people any spiritual joy or satisfaction in the belief and expectation of that blessedness. So it must be expected that his malice, heightened by the torment of his own guilt (which, as some think, are those chains of darkness in which he is kept for now, unto the judgment of the great day), will not and cannot leave this part of our happiness unattacked. He endeavours to supplant us of our birthright, our blessing, our salvation, and the comfortable hopes of these. From his common employment in this matter, Scripture has given him names that signify an opposition to Christ and his Spirit in the ways they take for our comfort and satisfaction. Christ is our Advocate who pleads for us; Satan is Diabolos [Διάβολος], a Calumniator. The Spirit intercedes for us; Satan is the Accuser [κατήγορος] of the brethren [τῶν ἀδελφῶν], who accuses them before God night and day. The Spirit is our Comforter; Satan is our Disturber, a Beelzebub who is ever raking in our wounds, as flies do upon sores. The Apostle Paul had this in view when he was advising the Corinthians to receive again the penitent incestuous person. His caution was most serious (2 Cor. 2. 11.), lest Satan get advantage of us, lest he deceive and outwit us (for his expression refers to men cunningly deceitful in trade, who overreach and defraud the unskilful). The reason for this caution was the known and commonly experienced subtlety of Satan, for we are not ignorant of his devices, implying that he will, and frequently does, lie in wait to take every advantage against us. Some indeed restrict these advantages to verse 10, as if Paul meant only that Satan was designing to fix in the Corinthians the opinion that backsliders into great sins were not to be received again, or that he laid a trap to raise a schism in the Church on account of this Corinthian. Others restrict the advantage he waited for to verse 7, where the Apostle expresses his fear lest the excommunicated person should be swallowed up with too much sorrow. But since the caution is not expressly tied to any one of these, it seems to point at them all, and to tell us that Satan drives many designs at once, and that in this man's case Satan would endeavour to push the Corinthians into a Pharisaical rigour, or to rend the Church by division over him, and to oppress the penitent by robbing him of his due comfort. So it still appears that it is one of his designs to hinder the comfort and trouble the hearts of God's children.

units.la: 1. Spiritual Comfort is the sweet Fruit of Holinefs, by which God adorns and beautifies the ways of Religious Service, to render them amiable and pleasant to the Undertakers, Her ways are ways of pleasantness, and all her paths are peace, Prov. 3. 17. and this is the present rest and refreshment of God's faithful Servants under all their toil, that when they have tribulation from the World, yet they have peace in him, Joh. 16. 33. and that being justified by Faith, they have peace with God, and sometimes joy unspeakable and full of glory, 1 Pet. 1. 8. and this they may the more confidently expect, because the fruits of the Spirit are Love, Joy, Peace, &c. Gal. 5. 22.
units.tr: 1. Spiritual comfort is the sweet fruit of holiness, by which God adorns and beautifies the ways of religious service, to make them lovely and pleasant to those who undertake them: Her ways are ways of pleasantness, and all her paths are peace (Prov. 3. 17.). This is the present rest and refreshment of God's faithful servants under all their toil: though they have tribulation in the world, yet they have peace in him (John 16. 33.); and being justified by faith, they have peace with God, and sometimes joy unspeakable and full of glory (1 Pet. 1. 8.). They may the more confidently expect this, because the fruits of the Spirit are love, joy, peace, etc. (Gal. 5. 22.).

units.la: 4. Spiritual Comfort is also a badg of our Heavenly Father's kindness. As Joseph (the Son of his Fathers affections) had a special testimony thereof in his party-coloured Coat; so have Gods Favourites a peculiar token of his good Will to them, when he gives them the Garments of Praise for the Spirit of Heaviness; if Spiritual Comfort be so advantagious to us, it will be no wonder to see Satan so much rage against it; it would be a satisfaction to him to tear these Robes off us, to impede so needful a Duty, to rob us of so much Strength, and to bereave us of the sweet fruits of our Labours.
units.tr: 4. Spiritual comfort is also a badge of our heavenly Father's kindness. As Joseph (the son of his father's affections) had a special token of it in his coat of many colours, so God's favourites have a peculiar sign of his goodwill toward them when he gives them the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness. If spiritual comfort is so advantageous to us, it is no wonder to see Satan rage so much against it. It would be a satisfaction to him to tear these robes from us, to hinder so needful a duty, to rob us of so much strength, and to deprive us of the sweet fruits of our labours.

units.la: Thirdly, It further appears that Satan's design is against the Comforts of God's Children, by the many advantages he hath against them, from the trouble and disquiet of their Hearts: I shall reckon up the chief of them; As,
units.tr: Thirdly, it further appears that Satan's design is against the comforts of God's children from the many advantages he gains over them through the trouble and disquiet of their hearts. I shall set down the chief of these.

units.la: 2. Disquiets of Heart unfit us for Duty, by hindering our activity in profecution of Duty. The whole Heart, Soul, and Strength should be engaged in all religious Services, but these Troubles are as Clogs and Weights to hinder motion. Joy is the dilatation of the Soul, and widens it for any thing which it undertakes; but Grief contracts the Heart, and narrows all the faculties: hence doth David beg an enlarged heart, as the principle of Activity, Psal. 119.32. I will run the way of thy Commandments, when thou shalt enlarge my Heart: for what can else be expected, when the Mind is so distracted with Fear and Sorrow, but that it should be uneven, tottering, weak, and confused? so that if it do set it self to any thing, it acts troublesomly, drives on heavily, and doth very little with a great deal ado; and yet were the unfitness the less, if that little which it can do, were well done, but the Mind is so interrupted in its endeavours, that sometimes in Prayer the Man begins, and then is presently at a stand, and dare not proceed, his words are swallowed up, he is so troubled that he cannot speak, Psal. 77.4. Sometimes the Mind is kept so imployed and fixed on Trouble that it cannot attend in Hearing or Praying, but presently the Thoughts are called off, and become wandring.
units.tr: 2. Disquiets of heart unfit us for duty by hindering our activity in pursuing it. The whole heart, soul, and strength should be engaged in all religious services, but these troubles are like clogs and weights that hinder movement. Joy is the dilatation of the soul, and it widens the soul for whatever it undertakes; but grief contracts the heart and narrows all the faculties. Hence David begs for an enlarged heart as the source of activity: Psal. 119.32. I will run the way of thy commandments, when thou shalt enlarge my heart. For what else can be expected when the mind is so distracted by fear and sorrow, than that it should be unsteady, tottering, weak, and confused? So if it does set itself to anything, it acts with difficulty, drives on heavily, and does very little with a great deal of ado. Yet the unfitness would be less if that little it can do were well done. But the mind is so interrupted in its endeavours that sometimes, in prayer, a man begins and is at once at a stand, and dares not go on: his words are swallowed up, he is so troubled that he cannot speak, Psal. 77.4. Sometimes the mind is so occupied and fixed on trouble that it cannot attend in hearing or praying, and the thoughts are at once called away and wander.

units.la: By all these ways doth the Devil, through the disquiet of Mind, unfit the Lord's People for Duty; and what a sad advantage this is against us cannot easily be told. By this means he may widen the distance betwixt God and us, keep our Wounds open, make us a reproach to Religion: And what not? But
units.tr: By all these ways the devil, through the disquiet of mind, unfits the Lord's people for duty; and what a sad advantage this gives him against us cannot easily be told. By this means he may widen the distance between God and us, keep our wounds open, and make us a reproach to religion: and what not? But

units.la: 4. Satan makes use of the troubles of Gods Children as a stumbling-block to others. 'Tis no small advantage to him, that he hath hereby an occasion to render the ways of God unlovely to those that are beginning to look Heaven-ward, he sets before them, the Sighs, Groans, Complaints, and restless Out-cries of the wounded in Spirit, to scare them off from all seriousness in Religion, and whispers this to them; Will you chuse a Life of Bitterness and Sorrow? can you eat Ashes for Bread, and mingle your Drink with Tears? will you exchange the comforts and contents of Life, for a melancholly Heart, and a dejected countenance? how like you to go Mourning all the day, and at night to be scared with Dreams and terrified with Visions? will you chuse a Life that is worse than Death? and a condition which will make you a terrour to your selves, and a burthen to others? can you be in love with an heart loaden with grief, and perpetual fears almost to distraction? while you see others in the mean time enjoy themselves in a contented peace? Thus he follows young beginn-ers with his suggestions, making them believe that they cannot be serious in Religion, but at last they will be brought to this, and that 'tis a very dangerous thing to be religious overmuch,and the high way to dispair: So that if they must have a Religion, he readily directs them to use no more of it, than may consist with the pleasures of Sin and the World, and to make an easy business of it, not to let Sin lye over-near their Heart, lest it disquiet them, nor over-much to concern themselves with Study, Reading, Prayer, or hearing of threatning awakening Sermons, lest it make them Mad, nor to affect the sublimities of Communion with God, exercises of Faith and Divine Love, lest it discompose them, and dash their worldly Jollities out of Countenance. A Counsel that is readily enough embraced by those that are almost perswaded to be Christians; and the more to confirm them in it, he sticks not sometime to asperse the poor troubled Soul with Dissimulation (where that accusation is proper, for the Devil cares not how inconsistent he be to himself, so that he may but gain his end) affirming all his seriousness to be nothing but whining Hypocrisy. So that whether they judge these troubles to be real or feigned, his conclusion is the same, and he perswades Men thereby to hold off from all religious strictness, holy diligence, and careful watchfulness.
units.tr: 4. Satan makes use of the troubles of God's children as a stumbling-block to others. It is no small advantage to him that he thereby has an occasion to make the ways of God unlovely to those who are beginning to look Heavenward. He sets before them the sighs, groans, complaints, and restless outcries of the wounded in spirit, to scare them off from all seriousness in religion, and whispers this to them: Will you choose a life of bitterness and sorrow? Can you eat ashes for bread, and mingle your drink with tears? Will you exchange the comforts and contents of life for a melancholy heart and a dejected countenance? How do you like going about mourning all day, and at night being scared with dreams and terrified with visions? Will you choose a life that is worse than death, and a condition that will make you a terror to yourself and a burden to others? Can you be in love with a heart loaded with grief and perpetual fears, almost to distraction, while you see others in the meantime enjoying themselves in contented peace? Thus he follows young beginners with his suggestions, making them believe that they cannot be serious in religion without being brought to this, and that it is a very dangerous thing to be religious overmuch, and the high road to despair. So if they must have a religion, he readily directs them to use no more of it than may consist with the pleasures of sin and the world, and to make an easy business of it: not to let sin lie too near their heart, lest it disquiet them; nor to concern themselves overmuch with study, reading, prayer, or hearing threatening, awakening sermons, lest it make them mad; nor to aspire to the sublimities of communion with God, the exercises of faith and divine love, lest it discompose them and dash their worldly jollities out of countenance. This is advice readily enough embraced by those who are almost persuaded to be Christians; and to confirm them in it, he does not hesitate now and then to charge the poor troubled soul with dissimulation (where that accusation fits, for the Devil does not care how inconsistent he is with himself, so long as he may gain his end), affirming all their seriousness to be nothing but whining hypocrisy. So whether they judge these troubles to be real or feigned, his conclusion is the same: he persuades men thereby to hold off from all religious strictness, holy diligence, and careful watchfulness.

units.la: 7. When 'tis at this height, the Devil hath but one Stage more, and that is the suggesting of irregular means for ease. Rage against God doth not quench the inward burning;Blasphemies against Heaven easeth not the Pain, the Soar runs still and ceaseth not, the trouble continues, the Man cannot endure it longer, all Patience and Hope is gone,what shall he do in this case? The Devil offers his Service, he will be the Physician, and commonly he prescribes one of these two things: 1. That 'tis best to endeavour to break through all this trouble into a resolved prophanenefs; not to stand in awe of Laws, nor to believe that there is a God that governs in the Earth, but that this is only the bitter fruit of melancholy, and unnecessary serioufnefs, and therefore 'tis best; to eat, drink, and be merry. If a Man can thus escape out of his trouble,the Devil needs no more; but oft he cannot, the wounds of Conscience will not be thus healed. Then, 2. He hath another remedy which will not fail,as he tells them, that is,to destroy themselves, to end their troubles with their lives. How open are the Breasts of troubled Creatures to all these Darts? and were it not that God secretly steps in, and holds the afflicted with his right hand, 'tis scarce imaginable but that wounded Consciences should by Satan's subtile improvement of so fair an advantage, be brought to all this misery.
units.tr: 7. When it is at this height, the Devil has but one stage more, and that is the suggesting of irregular means for ease. Rage against God does not quench the inward burning; blasphemies against Heaven do not ease the pain. The sore runs still and does not cease, the trouble continues, the man cannot endure it longer, all patience and hope is gone. What shall he do in this case? The Devil offers his service; he will be the physician, and commonly he prescribes one of these two things: (1) that it is best to endeavour to break through all this trouble into a resolved profaneness, not to stand in awe of laws, nor to believe that there is a God who governs the earth, but that this is only the bitter fruit of melancholy and unnecessary seriousness, and therefore it is best to eat, drink, and be merry. If a man can thus escape out of his trouble, the Devil needs no more; but often he cannot, for the wounds of conscience will not be healed in this way. Then (2) he has another remedy which will not fail, as he tells them, that is, to destroy themselves, to end their troubles with their lives. How open are the breasts of troubled creatures to all these darts! And were it not that God secretly steps in and holds the afflicted with his right hand, it is scarce imaginable but that wounded consciences should, by Satan's subtle improvement of so fair an advantage, be brought to all this misery.

units.la: 8. Satan can afflict the Body, by the Mind. For these two are so closely bound together, that their good and bad estate is shared betwixt them. If the Heart be merry, the Countenance is chearful, the Strength is renewed, the Bones do flourish like an Herb. If the Heart be troubled, the Health is impaired, the Strength is dryed up, the Marrow of the Bones wasted, &c. Grief in the Heart, is like a Moth in the Garment, it insensibly consumeth the Body, and disorderceth it. This advantage of weakening the Body falls into Satans hands by necessary consequence, as the Prophets ripe Figs, that fell into the Mouth of the Eater. And surely he is well pleased with it, as he is an Enemy both to Body and Soul: But 'tis a greater satisfaction to him, in that as he can make the Sorrows of the Mind, produce the Weaknes and Sicknes of the Body: So can he make the Distemper of the Body (by a reciprocal requital) to augment the trouble of the Mind. How little can a sickly Body do? it disables a Man for all Services, he cannot oft Pray, nor Read, nor Hear. Sickness takes away the Sweetnes and Comfort of Religious Exercises; this gives occasion for them to think the worse of themselves; they think the Soul is weary of the ways of God, when the Body cannot hold out. All failures which wearines and faintnes produce, are ascribed presently to the bad disposition of the Mind, and this is like Oyl cast upon the Flame. Thus the Devil makes a double gain out of Spiritual trouble.
units.tr: 8. Satan can afflict the body by the mind. For these two are so closely bound together that their good and bad estate is shared between them. If the heart be merry, the countenance is cheerful, the strength is renewed, the bones flourish like an herb. If the heart be troubled, the health is impaired, the strength is dried up, the marrow of the bones wasted, &c. Grief in the heart is like a moth in a garment: it insensibly consumes the body and disorders it. This advantage of weakening the body falls into Satan's hands by necessary consequence, as the prophet's ripe figs fell into the mouth of the eater. And surely he is well pleased with it, as he is an enemy both to body and soul. But it is a greater satisfaction to him that, as he can make the sorrows of the mind produce the weakness and sickness of the body, so he can make the distemper of the body, by a reciprocal requital, augment the trouble of the mind. How little can a sickly body do? It disables a man for all services: he cannot often pray, nor read, nor hear. Sickness takes away the sweetness and comfort of religious exercises; this gives occasion for them to think the worse of themselves; they think the soul is weary of the ways of God, when the body cannot hold out. All failures which weariness and faintness produce are presently ascribed to the bad disposition of the mind, and this is like oil cast upon the flame. Thus the Devil makes a double gain out of spiritual trouble.

units.la: CHAP. VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: HAving evidenced that one of Satan's principal designs is against the Peace and Comfort of God's Children; I shall next endeavour a discovery of the various ways by which he doth undermine them herein. All inward troubles are not of the same kind in themselves, neither doth Satan always produce the same effects out of all. Some being in their own nature disquiets, that do not so directly, and immediately overthrow the Peace and Joy of believing, and the Comforts of assurance of Divine Favour, as others do. Yet seeing that by all, he hath no small advantage against us, as to Sin and Trouble, and that any of them at the longrun, may lead us to question our interest in Grace, and the Love of God, and may accordingly afflict us, I shall speak of them all; which that I may do the more distinctly, I shall rank these troubles into several heads, under peculiar names, (it may be not altogether so proper, but that the curious may find matter of exception to them) that by them and their explanation, the differences may the better appear. I distinguish therefore of a fourfold trouble, that the Devil doth endeavour to work up upon the Hearts of Men. They are, 1. Discompofures. 2. Affrightments. 3. Dejections of Sadnefs. 4. Distresses of Horrour. Of all which I shall speak in their order. And
units.tr: Having shown that one of Satan's principal designs is against the peace and comfort of God's children, I shall next try to discover the various ways by which he undermines them. Not all inward troubles are of the same kind in themselves, and Satan does not always produce the same effects from all of them. Some are in their own nature disquiets which do not so directly and immediately overthrow the peace and joy of believing, and the comfort of assurance of God's favour, as others do. Yet since by all of them he gains no small advantage against us, both as to sin and as to trouble, and since any of them, in the long run, may lead us to question our interest in grace and in the love of God, and may accordingly afflict us, I shall speak of them all. So that I may do this more clearly, I shall group these troubles under several heads, with peculiar names (perhaps not altogether fitting, so that the curious may find something to object to), so that the differences may appear better through the names and their explanation. I therefore distinguish a fourfold trouble which the Devil endeavours to work up in the hearts of men. They are: 1. Discomposures. 2. Affrightments. 3. Dejections of sadness. 4. Distresses of horror. I shall speak of each in its order. And

units.la: 1. Of Discompofures of Soul. These are Molestations and Disturbances by which the Mind is put out of order and made unquiet; the calm (in which it should enjoy it self, and by which it should be composed to a regular and steady acting) being disturbed by a Storm of Commotion, and in which the Conscience or the peace of it is not presently concerned. This distinction of the trouble of Soul from the trouble of Conscience is not new, others have observed it before, and do thus explain it, Trouble of Soul is larger than trouble of Conscience; every troubled Conscience is a troubled Soul, but every troubled Soul is not a troubled Conscience: for the Soul may be troubled from Causes Natural, Civil, and Spiritual, according to variety of Occasions and Provocations, when yet a Man's inward peace with God is firm; and in some cases (as in Infants and in Men distracted with Feavers, &c.) there may be passions and disturbances of Soul, when the Conscience is not capable of exercising its office; nay the Soul of Christ was troubled (Joh. 12. 27. Now is my Soul troubled) when it was not possible that Sin or Despair should have the least footing in him.
units.tr: 1. Of disturbances of the soul. These are molestations and agitations by which the mind is thrown out of order and made restless. The calm in which it ought to rest and be composed for a regular and steady course of action is broken by a storm of commotion, and the conscience, or its peace, is not immediately involved. This distinction between trouble of the soul and trouble of conscience is not new; others have noted it before and explain it thus: trouble of the soul is wider than trouble of conscience. Every troubled conscience is a troubled soul, but not every troubled soul is a troubled conscience, for the soul may be troubled by natural, civil and spiritual causes, according to the variety of occasions and provocations, while a man's inward peace with God remains firm. In some cases, as in infants and in men driven out of their minds by fevers, there may be passions and disturbances of the soul when the conscience is not able to exercise its office. Indeed the soul of Christ was troubled (Joh. 12. 27. Now is my soul troubled) when it was impossible that sin or despair could have the least foothold in him.

units.la: For the opening of these discompofures of Soul, I shall, 1. Shew upon what advantage of Natural Temper the Devil is encouraged to molest Men. 2. By what occasions he doth work upon our Natural Inclinations. 3. And with what success of disturbance to the Soul.
units.tr: To open up these disturbances of the soul, I shall: (1) show what advantage of natural temper the devil uses to encourage him to molest men; (2) show by what occasions he works upon our natural inclinations; and (3) show with what success in disturbing the soul.

units.la: 2. Others have an envious Nature, always maligning and repining at other Mens felicity ; an evil Eye, that cannot look on anothers better condition without vexation. This turns a Man into a Devil, 'tis the Devil's proper sin, and the fury that doth unquiet him, and he the better knows of what avail it would be to help on our trouble.
units.tr: 2. Others have an envious nature, always grudging and repining at other men's happiness, with an evil eye that cannot look on another's better condition without vexation. This turns a man into a devil. Envy is the Devil's own sin, and it is the fury that unsettles him; he knows best how useful it would be to help on our trouble.

units.la: 6. And there are other Dispositions that are tender, to an excess of Sympathy, so that they immodcratly[?] affect and afflict themselves with other Mens sorrows. Though this be a temper more commendable than any of the former, yet Satan can take advantage of this, as also of the forenamed Dispositions, to discompose us, especially by suiting them with fit occasions which readily work upon these Tempers: And this was

Though this is a temper more commendable than any of the former, yet Satan can take advantage of it, as also of the aforementioned dispositions, to discompose us, especially by supplying them with fit occasions which readily work upon these tempers. And this was

units.la: 2. The second thing to be explained, which shall be performed by a brief enumeration of them, the chief whereof are these,
units.tr: 2. The second thing to be explained, which shall be done by a brief enumeration of them, the chief of which are these:

units.la: 5. To these may be added the pain or anguish of Sickness, and bodily Distemper. Though there are various degrees of pain, and that some Sickness are less afflictive than others, yet none of them forbear to pierce the Mind. The whole Man is discomposed; he that is exercised with strong pains upon his Bed, cryes out in the bitterness of his Soul, and he that by insensible degrees languisheth, grows ordinarily peevish, and his mind bleeds by an inward wound, so that he spends his days in sighing, and his years in mourning. And others there are, who being before acquainted with bodily pains, grow very impatient in Sickness, and are able to bear nothing: and besides the present sence of pain, the expectation of Death puts some into great commotion, the fears of it, (for it is naturally dreadful) fills them with disquiet thoughts, and those that approach to the Grave, by slow steps, under Consumption or languishing Sicknesses, they are habituated to sadnes, and can think of nothing chearfully, (except they have great assurance of Salvation, and have well learned to dye) because the Coffin, Grave, and Winding-sheet are still presented to them: these though they be very suitable Objects for Meditation, and (well improved) of great advantage for preparation to Death, yet doth Satan thereby (when it is for his purpose) endeavour to keep Men under grief, and to bereave them of their Peace.
units.tr: 5. To these may be added the pain or anguish of sickness and bodily disorder. Although there are various degrees of pain, and some sicknesses are less distressing than others, none of them fails to pierce the mind. The whole man is discomposed. He who is afflicted with strong pains upon his bed cries out in the bitterness of his soul, and he who wastes away by imperceptible degrees usually grows peevish, and his mind bleeds from an inward wound, so that he spends his days in sighing and his years in mourning. There are others who, having been acquainted with bodily pain before, grow very impatient in sickness and can bear nothing. Besides the present sense of pain, the expectation of death throws some into great turmoil; the fear of it (for it is naturally dreadful) fills them with disquieting thoughts. Those who approach the grave by slow steps, under consumption or wasting illnesses, become accustomed to sadness and can think of nothing cheerfully (unless they have great assurance of salvation and have learned well how to die), because the coffin, the grave and the winding-sheet are always placed before them. Although these are very suitable objects for meditation and, when rightly improved, of great advantage in preparing for death, Satan nevertheless uses them, when it serves his purpose, to keep men under grief and to deprive them of their peace.

units.la: 3. The third particular, promised to be explained for the discovery of these discompofures of Soul, was this; That by a concurrance of these and such like occasions, to such tempers, the Hearts of Men are disturbed, and their inward peace broken. This I shall evidence by these three things : 1. That these occasions meeting with such dispositions, do naturally raise great disturbances in their present working. 2. That they have a tendency to further trouble. 3. That Satan doth design, and hath it ordinarily in his power to discompose the Hearts of Men hereby.
units.tr: 3. The third point, promised to be explained for the discovery of these disturbances of soul, was this: that by a concurrence of these and similar occasions with such tempers, the hearts of men are disturbed and their inward peace broken. I shall demonstrate this by three things: 1. that these occasions, meeting with such dispositions, naturally raise great disturbances in their present working; 2. that they have a tendency to further trouble; 3. that Satan intends, and ordinarily has it in his power, to discompose the hearts of men in this way.

units.la: As to others, whose tempers are more apt to retain a troublesome Impression, 'tis very obvious that their discomposures have as much in length and breadth, as the other had in height. You may view Haman tormented under his secret discontent, which his Pride and Envy formed in him, for the want of Mordicai's Obeysance: the Kings Favour, a great Estate, high Honour, and what else a Man could wish to make him content, are all swallowed up in this Gulph, and become nothing to him. You see Amnon vexed and sick, for his Sister Tamer, waxing lean from day to day. You see Ahab (though a King, who had enough to satisfie his Mind) in the same condition for Naboth's Vineyard. If you say these were wicked Men, who rid their Lusts without a Bridle, and used the Spur: look then upon better Men, and you will see too much. Rachel so grieves and mourns for want of Children, that she professeth her Life inconsistent with her disappointment, Give me Children, else I die. Hanna upon the same occasion weeps and eats not, and prays in the bitterness of her Soul, and the abundance of her complaint and grief. Jeremiah (being pressed with discouragements from the contradiction of evil Men) calls himself a Man of strife and contention to the whole Earth, Jer. 15. 10. his sorrows thence arising, had so imbittered his Life, that he puts a woe upon his Birth, Wo is me,my Mother, that thou hast born me a Man of Strife. Paul had a noble courage under manifold afflictions, he could glory in the Cross, and rejoice in persecutions: nevertheless, the greatness of his work, the froward perverseness and unsteadiness of Professors, (which put him under fears, jealousies, and new travel) the Miseries of Christians, and the care he had for the concerns of the Gospel, (which was a constant load upon his Mind, his Heart (like old Eli's) trembling still for the Ark of God) made him complain as one worn out by the troubles of his Heart ; 2 Cor. 11.27. In wearinesse, and painfulnes, in watchings often, in hunger and thirst, in fastings often, in cold and nakednes. Besides those things that are without, that which cometh upon me daily, the care of all the Churches. Who is weak, and I am not weak? &c. For the Jews he had great heavinesse and continual sorrow in his Heart; and for the Gentiles he had perpetual fears.
units.tr: As to others, whose tempers are more apt to retain a troublesome impression, it is very obvious that their discomposures have as much in length and breadth as the others had in height. You may view Haman tormented under the secret discontent which his pride and envy formed in him for want of Mordecai's obeisance. The king's favour, a great estate, high honour, and whatever else a man could wish for to make him content, are all swallowed up in this gulf and become nothing to him. You see Amnon vexed and sick for his sister Tamar, waxing lean from day to day. You see Ahab (though a king, who had enough to satisfy his mind) in the same condition over Naboth's vineyard. If you say these were wicked men who rode their lusts without a bridle and used the spur, look then upon better men, and you will see too much. Rachel so grieves and mourns for want of children that she professes her life inconsistent with her disappointment: Give me children, else I die. Hannah, on the same occasion, weeps and eats not, and prays in the bitterness of her soul, in the abundance of her complaint and grief. Jeremiah, pressed with discouragements from the opposition of evil men, calls himself a man of strife and contention to the whole earth, Jer. 15. 10. His sorrows arising from this had so embittered his life that he puts a woe upon his birth: Woe is me, my mother, that thou hast borne me a man of strife. Paul had a noble courage under manifold afflictions; he could glory in the cross and rejoice in persecutions. Nevertheless, the greatness of his work, the froward perverseness and unsteadiness of professors (which put him under fears, jealousies and new travail), the miseries of Christians, and the care he had for the concerns of the gospel (which was a constant load upon his mind, his heart, like old Eli's, trembling still for the ark of God), made him complain as one worn out by the troubles of his heart: 2 Cor. 11.27. In weariness and painfulness, in watchings often, in hunger and thirst, in fastings often, in cold and nakedness. Besides those things that are without, that which cometh upon me daily, the care of all the churches. Who is weak, and I am not weak? etc. For the Jews he had great heaviness and continual sorrow in his heart, and for the Gentiles he had perpetual fears.

units.la: David was a Man that was often exercised with Sicknes and Troubles from Enemies, and in all the instances almost that we meet with in the Psalms, of these his Afflictions, we may observe the outward occasions of Trouble brought him under the suspition of Gods Wrath, and his Iniquity; so that he was seldom sick, or persecuted; but this called on the disquiet of Conscience, and brought his sin to remembrance; as Psal. 6. (which was made on the occasion of his Sicknes, as appears from verf. 5.) wherein he expresseth the vexation of his Soul under the apprehension[?] of Gods Anger; all his other griefs running into this Channel, (as little Brooks losing themselves in a great River) change their name and nature; he that was at first only concerned for his Sicknes, is now wholly concerned with sorrow and smart under the fear and hazard of his Souls condition; the like we may see in Psal. 38. and many places more.
units.tr: David was a man often exercised by sickness and by troubles from enemies. In nearly every instance of these afflictions that we meet in the Psalms, we can observe that the outward occasions of trouble brought him under the suspicion of God's wrath and his iniquity. He was seldom sick or persecuted without this stirring up disquiet of conscience and bringing his sin to remembrance. So in Psal. 6., which was written on the occasion of his sickness, as appears from verf. 5, he expresses the vexation of his Soul under the apprehension of God's Anger. All his other griefs run into this channel, as little brooks lose themselves in a great river, and change their name and nature. He who at first was concerned only for his sickness is now wholly concerned with sorrow and smart under the fear and hazard of his soul's condition. We may see the same in Psal. 38. and in many other places.

units.la: Having made good the assertion, That discomposures of Soul upon outward occasions, by long continuance and Satans management, do often run up to spiritual distress of Conscience: I shall next for further confirmation and illustration shew how it comesto be so.
units.tr: Having established that disturbances of the soul over outward causes, through long continuance and Satan's management, often rise into spiritual distress of conscience, I shall next, for further confirmation and illustration, show how this comes about.

units.la: 2. Discomposures of Soul afford the Devil fit matter to work upon. They furnish him with strong objections against sincerity of Holiness, by which the peace of Conscience being strongly assaulted, is at last overthrown. The usual Weapons by which Satan fights against the assurance of Gods Children, are the guilt of sins committed, and the neglect of Duty, and the disturbed Soul affords enough of both these to make a Charge against it self: For,
units.tr: 2. Discomposures of soul give the Devil fit matter to work upon. They furnish him with strong objections against sincerity of holiness, and by these the peace of conscience, being strongly assailed, is at last overthrown. The usual weapons with which Satan fights against the assurance of God's children are the guilt of sins committed and the neglect of duty, and the disturbed soul supplies enough of both to make a charge against itself. For:

units.la: 2. Discomposures obstructed Duties. This is the inconvenience which the Apostle(1 Pet.3.7.)tells us doth arise from disturbances among Relations; if the Wife or Husband do not carry well, so that discontents or differences arise, their Prayers are hindered. Duties.then are obstructed, 1. In the Act. When the Heart is out of frame, Prayer is out of season, and there is an averseness to it; partly because all good things are (in such confusions) burthensome to the Humor that then prevails, which eats out all desire and delight to spiritual things: and partly because they dare not come into Gods presence; conscience of their own guilt, and awe of God hindring such. approaches. 2. They obstruct the right manner of Performance, straitning the Heart, and contracting the Spirit, that if any thing be attempted, 'tis poorly and weakly performed. 3. And also the success of Duty is obstructed by discomposure. God will not accept such Services, and therefore Christ adviseth to leave the Gift before the Altar, (though ready for offering) where the Spirit is overcharged with Offences, or angry Thoughts, and first to go and be reconciled to our Brother, and then to come and offer the Gift, it being lost labour to do it before. From these sins of Omission and Commission, Satan can (and often doth) frame a dreadful charge against those that are thus concern'd, endeavouring to prove by these evidences, that they are yet (notwithstanding pretence of Conversion) in the gall of Bitterness, and bond of Iniquity, whereby the peace of Conscience is much shaken; and the more, because also
units.tr: 2. Disturbances obstruct duties. This is the inconvenience which the Apostle (1 Pet. 3.7.) tells us arises from discord among relations: if the wife or husband does not behave well, so that discontent or quarrels arise, their prayers are hindered. Duties are therefore obstructed in three ways. (1) In the act itself. When the heart is out of frame, prayer is out of season, and there is an aversion to it; partly because all good things are burdensome in such confusion to the humour that then prevails, which eats away all desire and delight in spiritual things; and partly because they dare not come into God's presence, the consciousness of their own guilt and the awe of God hindering such approaches. (2) They obstruct the right manner of performance, straitening the heart and contracting the spirit, so that if anything is attempted, it is performed poorly and weakly. (3) The success of duty is also obstructed by disturbance. God will not accept such services, and therefore Christ advises us to leave the gift before the altar (though it is ready for offering) where the spirit is overburdened with offences or angry thoughts, and first to go and be reconciled to our brother, and then to come and offer the gift, since it is lost labour to do it before. From these sins of omission and commission Satan can (and often does) frame a dreadful charge against those so concerned, endeavouring to prove by these evidences that they are still (despite any pretence of conversion) in the gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity, whereby the peace of conscience is much shaken; and all the more because also

units.la: 3. These discomposures of Soul give Satan a fit season for the management of his Accusation: Strong Accusations do often effect nothing, when the season is unsuitable. Many a time he hath as much to say against the Comforts of Men, when yet they shake all off (as Paul did the Viper off his hand) and feel no harm. But that which prepares the Conscience to receive the Indictment, is a particular disposition which it is wrought into, by suspicious credulity and fearfulness: These make the Heart (as Wax to the Seal) ready to take any impression that Satan will stamp upon it: Now by long disturbances he works the Heart into this Mould very often, and upon a double account he gains himself a fit opportunity to charge home his exceptions. 1. In that he sets upon the Conscience with his Accusations, after the Heart hath been long molested and confused with its other Troubles; for then the Heart is weakned and unable to make resistance as at other times. An Assault with a fresh Party after a long conflict, disorders its Forces, and puts all to flight. 2. In that long and great discomposures of Mind, bring on a distemper of Melancholy; for 'tis notoriously known by common experience, that those acid Humors (producing this distemper) which have their rise from the Blood, may be occasioned by their violent Passions of Mind, the Animal Spirits becoming inordinate (by long discomposures of Sadness, Envy, Terrour, and fretful Cares) and the motion of the Blood being retarded, it by degrees departs from its temperament, and is infected with an acidity, so that Persons no way inclined naturally to Melancholy may yet become so, by the disquiets of their troubled Mind.
units.tr: 3. These disturbances of soul give Satan a fit season for managing his accusation. Strong accusations often achieve nothing when the season is unsuitable. Many a time he has as much to say against men's comforts, yet they shake it all off (as Paul shook the viper off his hand) and feel no harm. But what prepares the conscience to receive the indictment is a particular disposition into which it is worked by suspicious credulity and fearfulness. These make the heart, like wax to a seal, ready to take any impression Satan will stamp upon it. Now by long disturbances he very often works the heart into this mould, and on a double account he gains for himself a fit opportunity to press home his objections. (1) He sets upon the conscience with his accusations after the heart has been long molested and confused by its other troubles; for then the heart is weakened and unable to make resistance as at other times. An assault by a fresh force after a long conflict disorders the defenders' ranks and puts all to flight. (2) Long and great disturbances of mind bring on a distemper of melancholy; for it is notoriously known from common experience that those acid humours (which produce this distemper) arising from the blood may be caused by violent passions of the mind, the animal spirits becoming inordinate through long disturbance of sadness, envy, terror and fretful cares. As the motion of the blood is retarded, it gradually departs from its temperament and is infected with acidity, so that persons not naturally inclined to melancholy may nonetheless become so through the disquiet of their troubled minds.

units.la: In our enquiries after Satan's success in working these discomposures of mind, we have discovered, 1. That the disturbances thence arising are great; 2. That they have a tendency to trouble of Conscience. There is but one particular more to be spoken of relating to his success in this design, and that is,

units.la: 3. 'Tis also a considerable ground of suspicion that Satan can do much in discomposures of Spirit, in that sometimes those whose tempers are most cool and calm, and whose singular dependance upon, and communion with God, must needs more strengthen them against these passionate vexations, are notwithstanding precipitated into violent commotions. Moses was naturally meek, above the common disposition of Men, and his very business was converse with God, whose presence kept his Heart under a blessed awe; yet upon the Peoples murmuring, he was so transported, with fullennefs and unbelief at the waters of Meribah, Numbers 20. 10, 12. that it went ill with him: which David thus expresseth, Psal. 106. 33. they provoked his Spirit, so that he spake unadvisedly with his Lips. Who can suppose less in this matter, than that Satan, having him at advantage, hurried him to this rashness? specially seeing such vehemencies were not usual with Moses, and that his natural temper led him to the contrary. This hath some affinity with the next consideration, Which is,
units.tr: 3. It is also a considerable ground for suspicion that Satan can do much to disturb the spirit. Sometimes those whose tempers are most cool and calm, and whose singular dependence upon and communion with God must surely strengthen them against these passionate vexations, are nevertheless thrown into violent commotions. Moses was naturally meek, above the common disposition of men, and his very business was converse with God, whose presence kept his heart under a blessed awe. Yet when the people murmured, he was so carried away with bitterness and unbelief at the waters of Meribah (Numbers 20:10, 12) that it went ill with him. David expresses this in Psalm 106:33: they provoked his spirit, so that he spoke unadvisedly with his lips. Who can suppose anything less in this matter than that Satan, having him at an advantage, hurried him into this rashness? This is especially so since such vehemence was not usual with Moses, and his natural temper led him the other way. This has some affinity with the next consideration, which is:

units.la: These general considerations amount to more than a suspition that it is much in Satan's power to give disturbances to the Minds of Men; yet for the clearer manifestation of the matter I shall shew, that he can do much to bring about occasions of discomposure, and also to stir up the Passions of Men upon these occasions.
units.tr: These general considerations amount to more than a suspicion that it is much in Satan's power to give disturbances to the minds of men. Yet for a clearer demonstration of the matter, I shall show that he can do much to bring about occasions of discomposure, and also to stir up the passions of men upon these occasions.

units.la: 1. By presenting the occasions worse than they are, or were ever intended,unjustly aggravating all circumstances. By this means he makes the object of the passions the more displeasing, and hateful; this must of necessity provoke to an higher degree.
units.tr: 1. By presenting the occasions worse than they are, or were ever intended, unjustly aggravating all the circumstances. By this means he makes the object of the passions more displeasing and hateful, and this must of necessity provoke them to a higher degree.

units.la: 2. He can in a natural way move (as it were) the Wheels, and set the passions a going, if they were of themselves more dull and sluggish: for he hath a nearer access to our Passions than every one is aware of. I will make it evident thus: our Passions, in their workings, do depend upon the fluctuations, excursions and rerecursions of the Blood, and animal Spirits, as Naturalists do determine: Now that Satan can make his approaches to the Blood, Spirits and Humors, and can make alterations upon them, cannot be denied, by those that consider what the Scripture speaks in Jobs case, and in the cases of those, that were by possession of the Devil, made Dumb, Deaf or, Epileptick: for if he could afflict Job with grievous Boils, 'tis plain he disordered and vitiated his Blood and Humors, which made them apt to produce such Boils or Ulcers; and if he could produce an Epilepsy, 'tis evident that he could infect the Lympha with such a sharpness, as by vellicating the Nerves, might cause a Convulsion: and these were much more than the disorderly Motions of Blood, Spirits or Humors which raise the passions of Men. If any object to this, That then (considering Satan's malicious diligence) we must expect the Passions of Men would never be at rest. 'Tis answered, that this power of Satan is not unlimited, but oft God prohibits him such approaches, (and without his leave he can do nothing); and also grace in God's Children, working calmness, submission and patience, doth ballance Satan's contrary endeavour. For as hurtful and vexatious occasions, being represented by the Sence to the imagination, are apt to move the Blood and Spirits: so on the contrary, the Ballast of Patience and other Graces, doth so settle the Mind, that the Blood and Spirits are kept steady in their usual course.
units.tr: 2. He can, in a natural way, move (as it were) the wheels and set the passions going, if they were of themselves more dull and sluggish, for he has a nearer access to our passions than everyone is aware of. I will make this evident thus: our passions, in their workings, depend upon the fluctuations, excursions and recursions of the blood and animal spirits, as the naturalists determine. Now, that Satan can make his approaches to the blood, spirits and humours, and can make alterations upon them, cannot be denied by those who consider what Scripture says in Job's case, and in the cases of those who, by possession of the Devil, were made dumb, deaf or epileptic. For if he could afflict Job with grievous boils, it is plain that he disordered and vitiated his blood and humours, which made them apt to produce such boils or ulcers; and if he could produce an epilepsy, it is evident that he could infect the lymph with such a sharpness that, by vellicating the nerves, it might cause a convulsion. These were much greater than the disorderly motions of blood, spirits or humours which raise the passions of men. If anyone objects that, then (considering Satan's malicious diligence), we must expect the passions of men would never be at rest, it is answered that this power of Satan is not unlimited; often God prohibits him such approaches (and without his leave he can do nothing); and also grace in God's children, working calmness, submission and patience, doth balance Satan's contrary endeavour. For as hurtful and vexatious occasions, being represented by the senses to the imagination, are apt to move the blood and spirits, so on the contrary the ballast of patience and other graces doth so settle the mind that the blood and spirits are kept steady in their usual course.

units.la: 3. When the Passions are up, Satan can by his suggestions make them more heady and violent. He can suggest to the Mind Motives and Arguments to forward it, and can stir up our natural corruption with all its powers to strike in with the opportunity. Thus he not only kindles the Fire, but blows the Flame.
units.tr: 3. When the passions are up, Satan can by his suggestions make them more heady and violent. He can suggest to the mind motives and arguments to forward them, and can stir up our natural corruption with all its powers to strike in with the opportunity. Thus he not only kindles the fire, but blows the flame.
