units.la: BEsides the troubles already mentioned under the heads of discomposures of Spirit, and affrightments, there is a third kind of trouble which Satan gives to the Children of God, and this may for distinction sake, be called Spiritual Sadness. These Spiritual Sadnesses are troubles raised in the Mind, relating to the Conscience, and Spiritual State or Condition of Men. They differ exceedingly from the two former sorts of trouble: for, 1. These troubles wholly concern the Conscience in point of Regeneration, and Men's suitableness thereunto; whereas simple discomposures of Spirit firstly relate to outward things. 2. In these the Conscience is immediately concerned, but in other troubles, the Conscience is either wholly untouched, or wounded only secondarily, by continuance and progress of the discomposure of the Spirit. 3. In these troubles, Conscience is the great instrument by which the Devil works, whereas in the trouble of affrightments the Devil acted alone, the Heart being in the mean time, uncomplyant and resisting. For the opening of this trouble, I shall explain, The several degrees thereof. 'Tis a trouble of Conscience unduly aggravated by Satan, wherein he confines himself to the operations of Conscience. But then, as he suggests the troubles of Men by the voice of Conscience, so he doth all he can to make it irregular in its actings, and excessive in that irregularity. So that in this case, the Conscience is evil, and imploys it self in that mistake, to enquire into Mens Regeneracy or Holiness, always being either a Neuter, or an Adversary, and the Devil helps this forward all he can.
units.tr: Besides the troubles already mentioned under the heads of discomposures of spirit and affrightments, there is a third kind of trouble which Satan gives to the children of God, and this may, for the sake of distinction, be called Spiritual Sadness. These spiritual sadnesses are troubles raised in the mind, relating to the conscience and the spiritual state or condition of men. They differ greatly from the two former sorts of trouble. (1) These troubles wholly concern the conscience with respect to regeneration and men's suitableness to it, whereas simple discomposures of spirit relate first of all to outward things. (2) In these the conscience is immediately concerned, whereas in other troubles the conscience is either wholly untouched, or wounded only secondarily, by the continuance and progress of the discomposure of the spirit. (3) In these troubles the conscience is the great instrument by which the devil works, whereas in the trouble of affrightments the devil acted alone, the heart meanwhile being uncompliant and resisting. To open up this trouble, I shall explain its several degrees. It is a trouble of conscience unduly aggravated by Satan, in which he confines himself to the operations of the conscience. But then, as he suggests the troubles of men through the voice of conscience, so he does all he can to make it irregular in its actings and excessive in that irregularity. So in this case the conscience is evil, and busies itself in that mistake, enquiring into men's regeneracy or holiness, always being either a neuter or an adversary, and the devil helps this forward all he can.

units.la: That the Conscience may be in such a Distemper, that it will not witness for a Man, when yet it cannot witness against him, is the observation of those that have treated of the nature of Conscience : Sometimes it will not make application of God's Promises, though it will believe, that he that forsakes Sin is regenerate, that he that truly repents shall be pardoned, yet it will not affirm for a Man, that he forsakes Sin or repents, though he really do so; or if it cannot deny that, yet it will sometimes refuse to make that conclusion which one would think would follow of it self, by natural consequence, and so refuseth to judge the Person regenerate or pardoned, though it cannot deny but that he forsakes Sin and repents. The greatness of the Blessing, the remainders of Unbelief, the deep sense of Unworthiness, with other considerations, do keep off the Heart from making (as I may say) so bold with the Promises; but all this while the Devil is doing his utmost to aggravate these considerations, afrighting the Conscience from that just absolution which it ought to give.
units.tr: That the conscience may be in such a distemper that it will not witness for a man, when yet it cannot witness against him, is the observation of those who have treated of the nature of conscience. Sometimes it will not make application of God's promises. It will believe that he who forsakes sin is regenerate, and that he who truly repents shall be pardoned, yet it will not affirm for a man that he forsakes sin or repents, though he really does so. Or, if it cannot deny that, it will sometimes refuse to draw the conclusion which one would think follows of itself by natural consequence, and so refuses to judge the person regenerate or pardoned, though it cannot deny that he forsakes sin and repents. The greatness of the blessing, the remainders of unbelief, the deep sense of unworthiness, and other considerations keep the heart from making (as I may say) so bold with the promises. But all this while the devil is doing his utmost to aggravate these considerations, frightening the conscience away from the just absolution which it ought to give.

units.la: 3. The third degree of trouble of Con-science is when the Conscience peremptorily denies the state of Regeneration. Hereby a Man that is really regenerate, is concluded to be yet in the Gall of bitterness, and bond of Iniquity; his former hopes are taxed for self-delusion, and his present state to be a state of Nature. This trouble is far greater than the two former; because the Party is judged to be in greater hazard, and by many degrees more remote from hope. 'Tis the frequent and sad thought of such, That if Death should in that estate cut off their days, Oh! then they were for ever miserable. The fears and disquiets of the Heart on this account, are very grievous, but yet they admit of degrees, according to the Ignorance of the Party, the Distemper of the Conscience, the Strength of the Objections, or Severity of the Prosecution, in regard the Conscience is now sadly out of order. We may call this degree of grief (for distinction) a wounded Spirit; which how hard it isto be born Solomon tells us, Prov. 18. 14. By comparing it with all other kind of troubles, which the Spirit of a Man can make some shift to bear, making this heavier than all, and above ordinary strength.
units.tr: 3. The third degree of trouble of conscience is when the conscience peremptorily denies the state of Regeneration. Hereby a man who is really regenerate is concluded to be still in the Gall of bitterness, and bond of Iniquity; his former hopes are taxed as self-delusion, and his present state is said to be a state of nature. This trouble is far greater than the two former, because the party is judged to be in greater hazard, and by many degrees more remote from hope. It is the frequent and sad thought of such that if death should cut off their days in that estate, oh! then they were for ever miserable. The fears and disquiets of the heart on this account are very grievous, but yet they admit of degrees, according to the Ignorance of the party, the Distemper of the conscience, the Strength of the objections, or the Severity of the prosecution, inasmuch as the conscience is now sadly out of order. We may call this degree of grief (for distinction) a wounded Spirit. How hard it is to bear, Solomon tells us (Prov. 18.14), by comparing it with all other kinds of troubles which the Spirit of a Man can make some shift to bear, making this heavier than all and above ordinary strength.

units.la: Some make enquiry what may be the difference betwixt a wounded Spirit, in the Regenerate and the Reprobate? To which it may be answered, 1. That in the Parties apprehension there is no difference at all: both of them may be compassed about with the Sorrows of Death, and suppose themselves to be in the Belly of Hell.
units.tr: Some make enquiry what the difference may be between a wounded spirit in the Regenerate and in the Reprobate. To which it may be answered: 1. In the party's apprehension there is no difference at all: both of them may be compassed about with the Sorrows of Death and suppose themselves to be in the Belly of Hell.

units.la: 2. For the further explanation whereof I shall next shew you that this is an usual trouble to the Children of God.
units.tr: 2. To explain this further, I shall next show that this is a common trouble among the children of God.

units.la: 2. The provisions which God hath made in his Word for such, is an evidence that such Distem-pers are frequent. He that in a City shall observe the Shops of the Apothecaries, and there take notice of the great variety of Medicines, Pots and Glasses full of Mixtures, Confection and Cordials: may from thence rationally conclude, that 'tis a frequent thing for Men to be Sick, though he should not converse with any Sick Person for his information. Thus may we be satisfied from the Declarations, Directions, and Consolations of Scripture, that 'tis a common case for the Children of God to stand in need of Spiritual Physitians, and Spiritual Remedies to help them, when they are wounded and fainting. Solomon's exclamination, a wounded Spirit who can bare? shews that the Spirit is sometimes wounded. The Prophets direction, he that walks in darkness and sees no Light, let him trust in the Lord, clearly implies that some there are that walk in darkness. God's creating the fruit of the Lips, Peace, peace; his promises of restoring Comforts to Mourners; his commands to others to comfort them; do all inform us, that 'tis a common thing for his Children to be under such Sadnesses of Spirit, that all this is necessary for their relief.
units.tr: Second, the provisions which God has made in his Word for such people are evidence that such distempers are frequent. Someone in a city who observes the shops of the apothecaries, and notes the great variety of medicines, pots and glasses full of mixtures, confections and cordials, may reasonably conclude from this that it is a frequent thing for men to be sick, even though he never speaks with any sick person for information. Thus we may be satisfied, from the declarations, directions and consolations of Scripture, that it is a common case for the children of God to need spiritual physicians and spiritual remedies to help them when they are wounded and fainting. Solomon's exclamation, "A wounded spirit who can bear?" shows that the spirit is sometimes wounded. The prophet's direction, "He that walks in darkness and sees no light, let him trust in the Lord," clearly implies that there are some who walk in darkness. God's creating "the fruit of the lips, peace, peace"; his promises of restoring comforts to mourners; his commands to others to comfort them: all these inform us that it is a common thing for his children to be under such sadness of spirit that all this is necessary for their relief.

units.la: 3. The reasons of this trouble, do also assure us of the frequency of it: for of them we may say (as Christ speaks of the poor) we have them always with us; so that the grounds of Spiritual Sadnes considered, 'tis no wonder to find many Men complaining under this Distemper. The reasons are,
units.tr: Third, the reasons for this trouble also assure us of its frequency: of them we may say (as Christ speaks of the poor) "we have them always with us." So, the grounds of spiritual sadness being considered, it is no wonder to find many men complaining under this distemper. The reasons are:

units.la: 1. The Malice of Satan, who hath no greater revenge against a Child of God, when translated from the Power of Darkness to the Kingdom of Christ, than to hinder him of the Peace and Comfort of that condition.
units.tr: (1) The malice of Satan, who has no greater revenge against a child of God, once translated from the power of darkness into the kingdom of Christ, than to deprive him of the peace and comfort of that condition.

units.la: Here it is requisite that I give satisfaction to this Query. Seeing that God doth sometime wound the Consciences of his Children, and that Satan also wounds them, what are the differences betwixt God and Satan, in inflicting these Wounds?
units.tr: Here it is requisite that I give an answer to this query. Since God sometimes wounds the consciences of his children, and Satan also wounds them, what are the differences between God and Satan in inflicting these wounds?

units.la: Answ. For the right understanding of this Question, I shall propound two things:
units.tr: Answer. For the right understanding of this question, I shall propound two things.

units.la: I have discovered the nature and degrees of these Spiritual Troubles, and that 'tis a common thing for the Children of God to fall under them. For the further opening of them, I shall next discover.
units.tr: I have described the nature and degrees of these spiritual troubles, and shown that it is a common thing for the children of God to fall under them. To open them further, I shall next discuss the occasions.

units.la: 3. The usual solemn occasions, that do as it were invite Satan, to give his onset against God's Children, and they are principally these Six.
units.tr: 3. The usual solemn occasions, which as it were invite Satan to make his onset against God's children, are chiefly these six.

units.la: 1. The time of Conversion: He delights to set on them when they are in the straits of a new Birth, for then the Conscience is awakned, the danger of Sin truly represented, fear and sorrow (in some degree) necessary and unavoidable. At this time he can easily overdrive them. Where the Convictions are deep and sharp, ready to weigh them down, a few Grains more cast into the Scale, will make the Trouble (as Job speaks) heavier than the Sand; and where they are more easie, or gentle, yet the Soul being unsetled, the thoughts in commotion, they are disposed to receive a strong impression, and to be turned (as Wax to the Seal) into a mould of Hopelesness and Desperation. That this is one of Satans special occasions, we need no other evidence for satisfaction, than the common experience of Converts; many of them do hardly escape the danger, and after their difficult Conquest of the troubles of their Heart, (which at that time are extraordinarily enlarged) do witnesse, that they are assaulted with desperate feares, that their sins were unpardonable, and sad conclusions against any expectation of favour from the Lord their God. These thoughts we are sure, the Spirit of God will not bear witnes unto because false, and therefore we must leave them at Satans door.
units.tr: 1. The time of conversion. He delights to set upon them when they are in the straits of the new birth, for then the conscience is awakened, the danger of sin is truly represented, and fear and sorrow (to some degree) are necessary and unavoidable. At this time he can easily overdrive them. Where the convictions are deep and sharp, ready to weigh them down, a few grains more cast into the scale will make the trouble (as Job speaks) heavier than the sand. Where the convictions are milder, yet the soul being unsettled and the thoughts in commotion, they are disposed to receive a strong impression and to be turned, as wax to the seal, into a mould of hopelessness and despair. That this is one of Satan's special occasions we need no other evidence than the common experience of converts. Many of them hardly escape the danger, and after their difficult conquest of the troubles of their heart (which at that time are extraordinarily enlarged), they bear witness that they are assaulted by desperate fears, that their sins were unpardonable, and that they had sad conclusions against any expectation of favour from the Lord their God. These thoughts, we are sure, the Spirit of God will not bear witness to, because they are false, and therefore we must lay them at Satan's door.

units.la: 6. Sickness, or Death-Bed, is another solemn occasion, which the Devil seldom misseth with his will. Death is a serious thing, it represents the Soul and Eternity to the Life. While they are at a distance, Men look slightly upon these, but when they approach near to them, Men usually have such a sight of them, as they never had before. We may truly call Sicknes and Death-Bed, an hour of Temptation, which Satan will make use of with the more mischievous industry, because he hath but a short time for it. That's the last Conflict, and if he miss that, we are beyond his reach for ever. So that in this case Satan incourageth himself to the Battel, with a now, or never. And hence we find, that it is usual for the dying Servants of God, to undergo most sharp Encounters; then to tell them (when the Soul is about to loose from the Body) that they are yet in their Blood, without God, and Hope, is enough to affright them into the extreamest Agonies; for they see no time before them answerable to so great a work, if it be yet to do. And withal, they are under vast discouragments from the wearinefs and pains of Sicknefs, their understandings and facultics being also dull, and stupified; so that if at this last plunge, God should not extraordinarily appear to rebuke Satan, and to pluck them out of these great Waters (as he often doth, by the fuller interposition of the Light of his Face, and the larger Testimony of his Spirit) after their long and comfortable profession of their Faith, and holy Walking, their Light would be put out in Darknes, and they would lie down in Sorrow.
units.tr: 6. Sickness, or Death-Bed, is another solemn occasion, which the Devil seldom misses to use for his purposes. Death is a serious thing: it sets the Soul and Eternity before the eyes of the living. While they are at a distance, men look lightly upon them, but when they draw near, men usually see them as they never saw them before. We may truly call Sickness and the Death-Bed an hour of Temptation, which Satan will use with all the more mischievous diligence because he has but a short time for it. That is the last conflict, and if he misses it, we are beyond his reach for ever. So in this case Satan rouses himself for the battle with now or never. Hence we find that it is common for the dying servants of God to undergo their most severe encounters. Then, to tell them (when the Soul is about to leave the Body) that they are still in their Blood, without God and without Hope, is enough to frighten them into the utmost agonies, for they see no time left before them adequate to so great a work, if it is still to be done. Besides, they are under great discouragements from the weariness and pains of sickness, their understandings and faculties also being dull and stupefied. So if at this last plunge God should not extraordinarily appear to rebuke Satan and pluck them out of these great waters (as he often does, by a fuller shining of the Light of his Face and a larger witness of his Spirit), then after their long and comfortable profession of faith and holy walking, their light would be put out in darkness, and they would lie down in sorrow.

units.la: 4.I have one thing more to add, for these discovery of these Spiritual Troubles, and that is to shew you the Engines by which Satan works them, and they are these two, Sophistry, and Fears.
units.tr: 4. I have one thing more to add concerning the discovery of these spiritual troubles, and that is to show you the engines by which Satan works them. They are these two: sophistry and fears.

units.la: 1. Scripture abused,and perverted. His way is not only to suggest that they are Unregenerate, or under an evil frame of Heart, but to offer proof that these Accusations are true. And because he hath to do with them that professes a belief of Scriptures, as the Oracles of God, he will fetch his proofs from thence; telling them that he will evidence what he saith from Scripture. Thus sometimes he assaults the weaker unskilful sort of Christians, Thou art not a Child of God: for they that are so, are Enlightned, translated from Darkness, they are the Children of the Light; but thou art a poor, ignorant, dark, blind Creature, and therefore no Child of God. Sometimes he labours to conclude the like, from the Infirmities of God's Children, abusing to this purpose, that of 1 John 3. 9. He that is born of God, doth not commit sin. And, He cannot sin, because he is born of God. Thus he urgeth it, Can any thing be more plainly and fully asserted? Is not this Scripture? Canst thou deny this? Then he pursues, But thou sinnest often, that is thine own complaint against thy self, thy Conscience also bearing witness to the truth of this Accusation; therefore thou canst be no Child of God. Sometimes he plays upon words that are used in divers senses, (a fit Engine for the Devil to work by) for what is true in one sense, will be false in another; and his arguing is from that which is true, to that which is false. I remember one that was long racked with that of Rev. 21. 8. The fearful and unbelieving, &c. shall have their part in the Lake, which burns with Fire and Brimstone. From whence the Party thus argued: The proposition is true; because 'tis Scripture, and I cannot deny the Assumption. Fearful I am, because I am doubtful of Salvation; and unbelieving I am, for I cannot believe that I am Regenerate, or in a state of Grace, and therefore I cannot avoid the Conclusion. To the same purpose he disputes against some, from 1 John 4. 18. There is no fear in love, but perfect love casteth out fear; but, thou art full of fears therefore thou lovest not God. Sometimes he makes use of those Scriptures, that make the prevailing degree of our love and respects to God, above the World, and the things of this Life, to be the Characters of true Grace; as that of John, If any Man love the World, the love of the Father is not in him: And that of Christ, If a Man love any thing more than Me, he is not worthy of Me: he that forsakes not all for Me, cannot be my Disciple, &c. Then he urgeth upon them their love of the World, and unwillingness to part with their Estates; and so brings the Conclusion upon them. Instances might be infinite, but by these you may judge of the rest. Let us now cast our Eye upon his subtilty, in managing his Arguments against men. 1. He grounds his Arguments on Scripture, because that hath authority with it, and the very troubled Conscience hath a reverence to it.
units.tr: 1. Scripture abused and perverted. His way is not only to suggest that they are unregenerate, or in an evil frame of heart, but to offer proof that these accusations are true. Because he has to do with those who profess belief in Scripture as the oracles of God, he will fetch his proofs from there, telling them he will prove what he says from Scripture. Thus he sometimes assaults the weaker, unskilled sort of Christians: Thou art not a child of God, for those who are so are enlightened and translated from darkness; they are the children of the light, but thou art a poor, ignorant, dark, blind creature, and therefore no child of God. Sometimes he labours to conclude the same from the infirmities of God's children, abusing to this purpose that text of 1 John 3. 9. He that is born of God doth not commit sin, and He cannot sin, because he is born of God. Thus he urges it: Can anything be more plainly and fully asserted? Is this not Scripture? Canst thou deny this? Then he pursues: But thou sinnest often; that is thine own complaint against thyself, thy conscience also bearing witness to the truth of this accusation; therefore thou canst be no child of God. Sometimes he plays upon words that are used in divers senses, a fit engine for the Devil to work by, for what is true in one sense will be false in another, and his arguing moves from what is true to what is false. I remember one who was long racked by that text of Rev. 21. 8. The fearful and unbelieving, etc. shall have their part in the lake which burns with fire and brimstone. From this the party reasoned thus: the proposition is true, because it is Scripture, and I cannot deny the assumption. I am fearful, because I am doubtful of salvation; and I am unbelieving, for I cannot believe that I am regenerate or in a state of grace; and therefore I cannot avoid the conclusion. To the same purpose he disputes against some from 1 John 4. 18. There is no fear in love, but perfect love casteth out fear: thou art full of fears, therefore thou lovest not God. Sometimes he uses those Scriptures which make the prevailing degree of our love and regard for God above the world and the things of this life the marks of true grace, such as that of John: If any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him, and that of Christ: If a man love any thing more than me, he is not worthy of me; he that forsakes not all for me cannot be my disciple, etc. Then he presses upon them their love of the world and their unwillingness to part with their estates, and so brings the conclusion upon them. The instances could be endless, but from these you may judge the rest. Let us now look at his subtlety in managing his arguments against men. First, he grounds his arguments on Scripture, because that has authority with them, and a troubled conscience has a reverence for it.

units.la: 2. He always suits his Scriptures, which he thus cites, to th[illegible, ~3 letters] wherein the Conscience is most tender: if there be any thi[?] that affords matter of suspition, or fear, he will be sure to [illegible, ~6 letters] such an Arrow out of the Quiver of Scriptures, as [illegible, ~2 letters] directly hit the Mark. 3. 'Though in the citation of Scripture, he always urgeth a sense which the Holy Ghost never intended: Yet there will be always something in those Scriptures which he makes use of, which in words at least, seem to favour his Conclusion; as appears in the Instances now given. For when he would conclude a Man not to be a Child of God because of his Ignorance, something of his Argument is true; it may be the Man is sensible that his knowledg is but little, compared with the measures which some others have; or that he is at a loss, or confused in many Doctrinal points of Religion; or hath but little experience in many Practical cases, &c. This, as it is true, so is it his trouble; and whilst he is poring upon his defect, Satan claps an Arrest upon him, of a far greater Debt than God chargeth upon him, and from Scriptures that speak of a total ignorance of the Fundamentals of Religion, (as that there is a God, that Christ Jesus is God and Man, the Redeemer of Mankind by a satisfaction to Divine Justice, &c.) Or of a wilful ignorance of the worth of the proffer of the Gospel, or its reality (which is discovered in the refusal of the terms thereof) he concludes him to be in a state of Darkness: whereas the Ignorance which the Man complains of, is not the Ignorance which those Scriptures intend. So in the next Instance, the sins which a Child of God complains of, are those of daily Incursion, which he labours and strives against; but that committing sin mentioned in the Text, hath respect to the Gnosticks, who taught a liberty in sinning, and fancied a Righteousness consistant with the avowed practice of Iniquity: Hence doth, John, directly face their Opinion, in these terms, Little Children, let no Man deceive you; he that doth Righteousness is righteous. And, He that is born of God neither doth, nor can, avouch a liberty of sinning; it being contrary to the Principles of the New Nature. So that the miscarriages of Infirmity which the Child of God laments in himself, are not the same with that of the Text, upon which Satan grounds the Accusation. The like may be said of the third Instance, from Rev. 21. 18. The threatning there is against such a fear to lose the comforts of the World, that they dare not believe the Gospel to be true, and accept it accordingly[?]: which is nothing to those fears and doubtings that may be[?] a Child of God, in reference to his Happinesse. Thus in all the [illegible, ~5 letters] the Fallacy lies in misapplying the Scripture (to suit them[?] to that[?] wherein the Conscience is tender,) under a sense which was never intended by them; yet in another sense, the thing charged upon the Conscience is true. 4. Yet is Satan so subtile, that when he disputes by such Fallacious Arguments, he chiefly endeavours to draw off the Defendants Eye and consideration, from that part of the Argument wherein its weakness lies (which in this case, is always in the abuse of the Scripture to a wrong sense); this he doth, partly from the advantage which he hath from the reverence that they carry to Scripture, they believe it to be true, and are not willing to suspect the sense; and many are so weak, that if they should, Satan is so cunning that he can easily baffle them in any distinction that they can make. And partly from thesense they have of that whereof they are accused, they feel themselves so sore in that place, (and for that very end doth Satan direct his Scripture to hit it) that they readily take it for granted, that the hinge of the Controversie turns upon it, and that the whole Dispute rests upon it. Now Satan having these fair advantages, by a further improvement of them, hides the weaknes of his Argument. For, 1. He takes that sense of the Scripture (in which he misapplies it) for granted, and that with great confidence, making as if there were no doubt there. 2. He turns always that part of the Argument to them, which they can least answer, pressing them eagerly with the matter of charge (which they are as ready to confess, as he isto accuse them of) and aggravating it very busily. And because the unskilful have no other direction for the finding the Knot of the Controversie, than Satan's busie, (though he, like the Lapwing, makes the greatest noise when he is furthest from his Nest, on purpose to draw them into a greater mistake) they look no further; and then not being able to answer, they are soon cast, and striking in with the conclusion against themselves, they multiply their Sorrows, and cry out of themselves as miserable.
units.tr: 2. He always fits the Scriptures he cites to the point where the conscience is most tender. If there is anything that gives cause for suspicion or fear, he will be sure to shoot such an arrow out of the quiver of Scripture as will hit the mark directly. 3. Though in citing Scripture he always urges a sense which the Holy Ghost never intended, there will always be something in the Scriptures he uses which, in words at least, seems to favour his conclusion, as appears in the instances just given. For when he would conclude that a man is not a child of God because of his ignorance, something in his argument is true: perhaps the man is aware that his knowledge is little, compared with the measure others have; or that he is at a loss, or confused in many doctrinal points of religion; or has little experience in many practical cases, etc. This, as it is true, is also his trouble; and while he is poring over his defect, Satan lays an arrest on him for a far greater debt than God charges him with, and does so from Scriptures that speak of a total ignorance of the fundamentals of religion (such as that there is a God, that Christ Jesus is God and man, the Redeemer of mankind by a satisfaction to divine justice, etc.), or of a wilful ignorance of the worth of the offer of the Gospel, or of its reality (which is shown in the refusal of its terms). He concludes that the man is in a state of darkness; yet the ignorance the man complains of is not the ignorance those Scriptures intend. So in the next instance, the sins a child of God complains of are those of daily incursion, which he labours and strives against; but the committing of sin mentioned in the text has respect to the Gnostics, who taught a liberty in sinning and imagined a righteousness consistent with the avowed practice of iniquity. Hence John directly confronts their opinion in these words: Little children, let no man deceive you; he that doeth righteousness is righteous. And: He that is born of God neither doth, nor can, sin; this asserts no liberty of sinning, it being contrary to the principles of the new nature. So the failings of infirmity which the child of God laments in himself are not the same as the sin in the text on which Satan grounds the accusation. The same may be said of the third instance, from Rev. 21. 18. The threat there is against such a fear of losing the comforts of the world that men dare not believe the Gospel to be true and accept it accordingly; this is nothing to the fears and doubts that may trouble a child of God concerning his happiness. Thus in all of [illegible], the fallacy lies in misapplying the Scripture, fitting it to that wherein the conscience is tender, under a sense which was never intended by it; yet in another sense, the thing charged upon the conscience is true. 4. Yet Satan is so subtle that, when he argues by such fallacious reasoning, he chiefly labours to draw the defendant's eye and attention away from that part of the argument where its weakness lies (which in this case is always the abuse of Scripture to a wrong sense). He does this partly from the advantage he gains through the reverence people have for Scripture: they believe it to be true and are unwilling to suspect the sense; and many are so weak that, if they did, Satan is so cunning that he can easily baffle them in any distinction they can make. And partly from the sense they have of what they are accused of: they feel themselves so sore at that point (and for that very purpose Satan directs his Scripture to hit it) that they readily take it for granted that the hinge of the controversy turns upon it, and that the whole dispute rests upon it. Now Satan, having these fair advantages, hides the weakness of his argument by further exploiting them. For, 1. he takes that sense of the Scripture (in which he misapplies it) for granted, and does so with great confidence, acting as if there were no doubt there. 2. He always turns against them that part of the argument which they can least answer, pressing them eagerly with the matter of charge (which they are as ready to confess as he is to accuse them of) and aggravating it very busily. And because the unskilful have no other guide for finding the knot of the controversy than Satan's busyness (though he, like the lapwing, makes the greatest noise when he is furthest from his nest, precisely to lead them into a greater mistake), they look no further*; and then, not being able to answer, they are soon cast, and, falling in with the conclusion against themselves, they multiply their sorrows and cry out that they are miserable.

units.la: ’Tis scarce possible to number the false Notions which are already entertained among Christians, relating to Grace and Conversion, much less those that may afterward arise. But I shall mention some that Satan frequently makes use of, as grounds of Objection.
units.tr: It is scarcely possible to count the false notions already held among Christians about grace and conversion, much less those that may arise later. But I shall mention some that Satan frequently uses as grounds of objection.

units.la: 1. ’Tis a common apprehension among the weaker sort, that Conversion is always accompanied with great fear and terrour. This is true in some (as hath been said); and though none of the Preachers of the Gospel have asserted the universality of these greater measures of Trouble, yet the People taking notice, that many speak of their deep humiliations in Conversion; and that several Authors have set forth the greatness of Distress that some have been cast into on that occasion, (though without any intention of fixing this into a general Rule) have from thence supposed, that all the Converted are brought to their Comforts through the flames of Hell. Upon this mistake, the Devil disquiets those that have not felt these extream Agonies of Sorrow in themselves; and tells them that it is a sure sign that they are not yet Converted. Though ’tis easie for a Man that sees the falshood of the Notion, to answer the Argument, yet he that believes it to be true, cannot tell what to say, because he finds he never was under such Troubles, and now he begins to be troubled because he was not troubled before, or (as he supposeth) not troubled enough.
units.tr: 1. It is a common belief among the weaker sort that conversion is always accompanied by great fear and terror. This is true in some cases (as has been said). Although none of the preachers of the Gospel has asserted that these greater measures of trouble are universal, the people notice that many speak of their deep humiliations in conversion, and that several authors have described the greatness of the distress that some have been cast into on that occasion (though without any intention of fixing this as a general rule). From this they have supposed that all the converted are brought to their comforts through the flames of Hell. On this mistake the Devil disquiets those who have not felt these extreme agonies of sorrow in themselves, and tells them that it is a sure sign that they are not yet converted. Though it is easy for a man who sees the falsehood of the notion to answer the argument, he who believes it to be true cannot tell what to say. He finds that he never underwent such troubles, and now he begins to be troubled because he was not troubled before, or (as he supposes) not troubled enough.

units.la: Note: none.
units.tr: Note: none.

units.la: 2. Another false Notion is, That a Convert can give an account of the time and manner of his Conversion. This is true in some, as in Paul, and some others, whose Change hath been sudden and remarkable, though in many this is far otherwise; who can better give account that they are Converted, than by what Steps, Degrees, and Methods, they were brought to it. But if any of these receive the Notion, they will presently find that Satan will turn the edge of it against them,and will tell them that they are not Converted, because they cannot nominate the time when, nor the manner how such a Change was wrought.
units.tr: 2. Another false notion is that a convert can give an account of the time and manner of his conversion. This is true in some, as in Paul and a few others, whose change was sudden and remarkable. But in many cases it is quite otherwise: such people can better say that they are converted than describe by what steps, degrees, and methods they were brought to it. But if any of these receive the notion, they will presently find that Satan turns its edge against them, and tells them that they are not converted, because they cannot name the time or the manner in which such a change was wrought.

units.la: 3. Some take it for granted, that Conversion is accompanied with a remarkable measure of Gifts for Prayer and Exhortation; and then the Devil objects it to them, That they are not Converted, because they cannot Pray as others, or Speak of the things of God so readily, fluently, and affectionately, as some others can. Thus the poor weak Christian is baffled for want of Abilities to express himself to God and Men.
units.tr: 3. Some take it for granted that conversion is accompanied by a remarkable measure of gifts for prayer and exhortation. Then the Devil objects to them that they are not converted, because they cannot pray as others do, or speak of the things of God as readily, fluently, and affectionately as some others can. Thus the poor, weak Christian is baffled for want of abilities to express himself to God and men.

units.la: 5. Some take it for a truth, that growth of Grace is always visible, and the progress remarkable. And then because they can make no such discovery of themselves, the Devil concludes their Grace to be counterfeit and hypocritical.
units.tr: 5. Some take it as a truth that the growth of grace is always visible, and its progress remarkable. Then, because they can discover no such growth in themselves, the Devil concludes that their grace is counterfeit and hypocritical.

units.la: 3. The third piece of Satan's Sophistry, from whence he raiseth false Conclusions, is his misrepresentation of God. In this he directly crosseth the design of the Scriptures, where God in his Nature, and Dealings is so set forth, that the Weakest, the most Afflicted and Tossed, may receive incouragement of Acceptance, and of his Fatherly Care over them in their saddest Tryals. Yet withal, lest Men should turn his Grace into Wantonness, and embolden themselves in sin because of his Clemency, the Scriptures sometimes give us lively descriptions of his Anger against those that wickedly presume upon his Goodness, and continue so to do. Both these Descriptions of God should be taken together, as affording the only true Representation of him. He is so gentle to the humbled sensible Sinner, that He will not break their bruised Reed, nor quench their smoking Flax. And so careful of Health, that (for their recovery) he will not leave them altogether unpunished; nor suffer them to ruine themselves by a Surfeit upon worldly Comforts; yet with the froward he will shew himself froward, Psal.18.26. And, As for such as turn aside unto their crooked ways, the Lord shall lead them forth with the workers of Iniquity, Psal.125.5. He will put out the Candle of the wicked, for he sets them in slippery places: So that they are cast down into Destruction, and brought into Desolation as in a moment; they are consumed with Terrours. Now Satan will sometimes argue against the Children of God, and endeavour to break their hopes, by turning that part of the Description of God against them; which is intended for the dismounting of the confidence of the Wicked, and the bringing down of high looks. By this means he wrests the Description of God to a contrary end, and misrepresents God to a trembling afflicted Soul. This he doth,
units.tr: 3. The third piece of Satan's sophistry, from which he draws false conclusions, is his misrepresentation of God. In this he directly opposes the design of the Scriptures, where God, in his nature and dealings, is so set forth that the weakest, the most afflicted and tossed, may receive encouragement to come to him, and to trust his fatherly care over them in their saddest trials. Yet, lest men should turn his grace into wantonness and embolden themselves in sin because of his clemency, the Scriptures sometimes give us vivid descriptions of his anger against those who wickedly presume upon his goodness and persist in doing so. Both of these descriptions of God should be taken together, as giving the only true representation of him. He is so gentle to the humbled, sensible sinner that he will not break their bruised reed, nor quench their smoking flax. And he is so careful of their health that, for their recovery, he will not leave them altogether unpunished, nor suffer them to ruin themselves by a surfeit of worldly comforts. Yet with the froward he will show himself froward, Psal. 18.26. And, As for such as turn aside unto their crooked ways, the Lord shall lead them forth with the workers of iniquity, Psal. 125.5. He will put out the candle of the wicked, for he sets them in slippery places; so that they are cast down into destruction, and brought into desolation as in a moment; they are consumed with terrors. Now Satan will sometimes argue against the children of God and try to break their hopes by turning that part of the description of God against them, which is intended to dismount the confidence of the wicked and bring down their haughty looks. By this means he twists the description of God to a contrary end and misrepresents God to a trembling, afflicted soul. He does this,

units.la: 4. Another common head from whence this great Disputant doth fetch his Arguments against the good condition and state of God's Servants, is their sin and miscarriages. Here I shall observe two or three things in the general concerning this, before I shew how he draws his false Conclusions from thence. As,
units.tr: 4. Another common head from which this great Disputant fetches his arguments against the good condition and state of God's Servants is their sin and miscarriages. Here I shall observe two or three things in general about this before I show how he draws his false conclusions from it. As,

units.la: 1. That with a kind of feigned ingenuity, he will grant a difference betwixt Sin and Sin, betwixt Sins reigning, and not reigning; Sins mortified, and not mortified; betwixt the Sins of the Converted, and the Unconverted: and upon this supposition he usually proceeds. He doth not always ( except in case of great Sins) argue want of Regeneration from one Sin for that Argument ; This is a Sin, therefore thou art not a Convert, would be easily anfwered, by one that knows the Saints have their imperfections but he thus deals with Men : These Sins whereof thou art guilty, are reigning Sins, such as are inconsistent with a converted estate, and therefore thou art yet unregenerated.
units.tr: 1. With a kind of feigned ingenuity, he will grant a difference between sin and sin: between sins reigning and not reigning, sins mortified and not mortified, and between the sins of the converted and of the unconverted. Upon this supposition he usually proceeds. He does not always (except in the case of great sins) argue want of regeneration from one sin. The argument This is a sin, therefore thou art not a convert would be easily answered by anyone who knows that the saints have their imperfections. But he deals with men thus: These sins whereof thou art guilty are reigning sins, such as are inconsistent with a converted estate, and therefore thou art yet unregenerate.

units.la: While Satan doth insist upon Arguments from the Sins of Believers, for the proof of an unconverted estate, he only aims to make good this point, That their Sins are reigning Sins, and consequently that they cannot be in so good a condition as they are willing to think. And to make their Sins to carry that appearance, his constant course is to aggravate them all he can: this is his design, and the means by which he would effect it. His great Art in this case, is to heighten the Sins of the Regenerate; this he doth many ways. As,
units.tr: While Satan insists upon arguments from the sins of believers, to prove an unconverted estate, he aims only to make good this point: that their sins are reigning sins, and consequently that they cannot be in so good a condition as they are willing to think. To make their sins carry that appearance, his constant course is to aggravate them all he can. This is his design, and the means by which he would effect it. His great art in this case is to heighten the sins of the regenerate, and he does this in many ways. As,

units.la: 1. From the nature of the Sin committed, and the manner of its commission: and this he chiefly labours, because his Arguments from hence are more probable, especially considering what he fixeth upon usually, is that which may most favour his Conclusion. A
units.tr: 1. From the nature of the sin committed and the manner of its commission. This he chiefly labours at, because his arguments from it are more plausible, especially as what he fixes upon is usually that which may most favour his conclusion. A

units.la: 2. He aggravates the sinfulness of our condition, from the frequency and violence of his own Temptations. 'Tis an usual thing for him to give a young Converts,incessant onsets of Temptation to Sin: most commonly he works upon their natural constitution, he blows the Coals that are not yet quite extinguished, and that have greater forwardness from their own inclination to kindle again; as Lust and Passion. The first motions of the one, (though it go no further, than those offers and risings up in the Heart, and is there damped, and kept down by the opposing principle of Grace) and the occasional out-breakings of the other, (which he provokes by a diligent preparation of occasion from without, and violent incitations from within) furnish him with sufficient matter for his intended accusations; and sometimes (being as it were wholly negligent of the advantages which our tempers give him, or not being able to find any such forwardness to these evils in our Constitution, as may more eminently serve his ends) he satisfies himself to molest us with earnest motions to any Sins indifferently; and all this to make us believe, that Sin is not crucified in us. Which some are more apt to believe, because they observe their Temptations to these Sins, to importune them more, and with greater vehemency than they were wont to do before: and this doth yet the more astonish them, because they had high expectations that after their conversion, Satan would fall before them, and their Temptations abate; that their natures should be altered, and their natural inclinations to these Sins wholly cease: but now finding the contrary, they are ready to cry out, (especially when Satan violently buffets them with this objection) We are yet in our Sins, and under the dominion thereof; neither can it be that we are converted, because we find Sin more active and stirring than formerly; 'tis not then surely mortified in us, but lively and strong. Though in this case it be very plain that Temptations are only strong, and Sin weak, and that Grace is faithfully acting its part against the Flesh, arguing, not that Grace is so very weak, but that Satan Is more busy than ordinary; the Sins are not more than formerly, but the Light that discovers them more is greater, and the Conscience that resents the Temptation is more tender. Yet all this doth not at first give ease to the fears that are now raised up in the Mind; they find Sin working in them, their expectations of attaining a greater conquest on a sudden, and with greater ease,are disappointed, (and the desire of having much, makes a Man think himself poor); and withal they commonly labour under so much Ignorance, or perverse credulity, that they conclude they consent to every thing which they are tempted to, insomuch that 'tis long before these Clouds do vanish, and the afflicted brought to a right understanding of themselves.
units.tr: 2. He aggravates the sinfulness of our condition by the frequency and violence of his own temptations. It is a common thing for him to launch incessant onsets of temptation to sin against young converts. Most often he works on their natural constitution; he blows on the coals that are not yet quite extinguished and that burn more readily from their own inclination to kindle again, such as lust and passion. The first motions of the one (though they go no further than those offers and risings-up in the heart, and are there damped and kept down by the opposing principle of grace), and the occasional outbreakings of the other (which he provokes by diligently preparing occasion from without and violent incitations from within), furnish him with sufficient material for his intended accusations. Sometimes, being almost careless of the advantages which our tempers give him, or unable to find in our constitution any such forwardness to these evils as would serve his purposes more eminently, he is content to harass us with earnest motions to any sins at all, and all this to make us believe that sin is not crucified in us. Some are the more ready to believe this because they observe their temptations to these sins to press more and with greater vehemency than they did before. This astonishes them all the more, because they had high expectations that after their conversion Satan would fall before them and their temptations would abate; their natures would be changed and their natural inclinations to these sins would wholly cease. But finding the contrary, they are ready to cry out (especially when Satan violently buffets them with this objection): We are still in our sins and under their dominion; nor can it be that we are converted, because we find sin more active and stirring than formerly. Surely it is not mortified in us, but lively and strong. Yet in this case it is very plain that the temptations are only strong and the sin weak, and that grace is faithfully acting its part against the flesh, which shows not that grace is so very weak, but that Satan is more busy than usual. The sins are not more than formerly, but the light that discovers them is greater, and the conscience that feels the temptation is more tender. Yet all this does not at first ease the fears now raised in the mind. They find sin working in them; their expectations of winning a greater conquest suddenly and with greater ease are disappointed (and the desire to have much makes a man think himself poor). Moreover, they commonly labour under so much ignorance or perverse credulity that they conclude they consent to everything to which they are tempted. So it is long before these clouds vanish and the afflicted are brought to a right understanding of themselves.

units.la: 5. The last part of Satan's Sophistry, is to lessen their Graces, that so he may altogether deny them. In this he proceeds upon such Scriptures, as do assert the Fruits of the Spirit; and urgeth for his foundation, that none are the Children of God, but such as are led by the Spirit; and that he that hath not the Spirit of Christ, is none of his. The necessity of Faith, Love, Patience, Humility, with the Fruits of these and other Graces, he presseth, but still in order to a Demonstration (as he pretends) that such are not to be found in those, whose Gracious state he calls into question, and consequently that they are not the Children of God.
units.tr: 5. The last part of Satan's sophistry is to lessen their graces, so that he may altogether deny them. In this he relies on such Scriptures as assert the fruits of the Spirit, and he urges as his foundation that none are the children of God except those who are led by the Spirit, and he that hath not the Spirit of Christ, is none of his. He presses the necessity of faith, love, patience and humility, together with the fruits of these and other graces, but always in order to a demonstration (as he pretends) that such graces are not to be found in those whose gracious state he calls into question, and consequently that they are not children of God.

units.la: The Rule by which he manageth himself in this Dispute, is this: The more Graces are heightned in the Notions, that must give an account of their Nature and Beings; the more difficult it will be to find out their Reality in the Practice of them. His design then hath these two parts. 1. He heightens Grace in the Notion, or Abstract, all he can. 2. He lessens it in the Concrete, or Practice, as much as is possible, that it may appear a very Nullity, a shadow and nota substance. I shall speak a little of both.
units.tr: The rule by which he conducts himself in this dispute is this: The more graces are heightened in the notions that must give an account of their nature and being, the more difficult it will be to find their reality in the practice of them. His design therefore has two parts. 1. He heightens grace in the notion, or abstract, as far as he can. 2. He lessens it in the concrete, or practice, as far as is possible, so that it may appear a mere nullity, a shadow and not a substance. I shall speak a little about both.

units.la: 2. Grace hath sometimes its special Assistances; this is when the occasion is extraordinary, but the Grace befitting that occasion is promised in ordinary, and ordinarily recieved. When God calls any to such occasions, though compared with that measure of Grace, which usually is acted by the Children of God upon ordinary occasions; it is a special assistance of the Spirit. Of this nature, is that Boldnes which the Servants of Christ receive, to confess Christ before Men in times of Persecution, and to Die for the Truth, with Constancy, Courage, and Joy. 3. There are also singular Eminencies of Grace, which some diligent, careful, and choice Servants of God attain unto, far above what the ordinary sort arrive at. Enoch had his Conversation so much in Heaven, that he was said to walk with God. David's Soul was often full of delight in God. Some in the height of Assurance, rejoyce in God, with joy unspeakable, and full of Glory. Moses was eminent in Meekness; Job in Patience; the Apostle Paul in Zeal, for promoting the Gospel, &c. Now Satan, when he comes to question the Graces of Men, he presents them with these Measures; and if they fall short, (as ordinarily they do) he concludes them altogether Gracelefs.
units.tr: 2. Grace sometimes has its special assistances. This is when the occasion is extraordinary, but the grace befitting that occasion is promised in ordinary and ordinarily received. When God calls anyone to such occasions, it is a special assistance of the Spirit, though compared with that measure of grace which the children of God usually exercise on ordinary occasions. Of this kind is that boldness which the servants of Christ receive to confess Christ before men in times of persecution, and to die for the truth with constancy, courage, and joy. 3. There are also singular eminences of grace, which some diligent, careful, and choice servants of God attain, far above what the ordinary sort reach. Enoch had his conversation so much in heaven that he is said to have walked with God. David's soul was often full of delight in God. Some, in the height of assurance, rejoice in God with joy unspeakable and full of glory. Moses was eminent in meekness, Job in patience, the Apostle Paul in zeal for promoting the Gospel, etc. Now when Satan comes to question men's graces, he presents them with these measures, and if they fall short (as ordinarily they do), he concludes they are altogether graceless.

units.la: 1. He gives us a description of Grace as it is in it self, abstracted from the Weaknes, Dulnes, Distraction, and Infirmities that are Concomitant with it, as it comes forth to Practice. He brings to our view Grace in its Glory, and without the Spots by which our Weaknes, and Satan's Temptation, do much disfigure it.
units.tr: 1. He gives us a description of grace as it is in itself, abstracted from the weakness, dullness, distraction, and infirmities that accompany it as it comes forth into practice. He brings before our eyes grace in its glory, without the spots by which our weakness and Satan's temptations greatly disfigure it.

units.la: 2. With these heights of common Grace, he compares the lowest degree of Special Grace. And because the Principles, Motives, and Ends, which constitute the difference betwixt these two, are (as it were) under-ground, more remote from Sense and Observation, and oftentimes darkned by Temptation : He takes the boldness to deny the Truth of Grace, upon the account of the small inconsiderable appearance that it makes, confidently affirming, that Special Grace must of necessity make a far greater outward shew than these Common Graces. In what manner, and to what end, Satan doth heighten Grace in the abstract we have seen : It remains that we discover,
units.tr: 2. With these heights of common grace he compares the lowest degree of special grace. And because the principles, motives, and ends which make the difference between these two are, as it were, underground, more remote from sense and observation, and often darkened by temptation, he takes the boldness to deny the truth of grace on account of the small and inconsiderable appearance it makes, confidently affirming that special grace must of necessity make a far greater outward show than these common graces. In what manner, and to what end, Satan heightens grace in the abstract we have seen. It remains that we discover:

units.la: 2. How he doth lessen Grace in the Concrete ; this is the center of his Design. He would not extol Grace so much, but that he hopes thereby to condemn the Generation of the Just, and to make it appear, that there are few or none, that are truly Gracious. When he comes to apply all this to the condition of any Child of God, he deals treacherously ; and his cunning consists of three Parts.

units.la: 3. When their Hearts are discomposed, or muddied with fear; for then their sight is bad, and they can so little judg of things that differ, that Satan can impose almost any thing upon them.
units.tr: 3. When their hearts are discomposed or muddied with fear, for then their sight is poor, and they can judge so little between things that differ that Satan can impose almost anything upon them.

units.la: 2. The other Engine by which he fixeth these Conclusions, which though it be not Argumentative, yet it serves to sharpen all his Fallacies against the Comforts of God's Children ; this is fear, which together with his Objections he sends into the Mind. That Satan can raise a storm and commotion in the Heart by fear, hath been proved before. I shall now only in a few things shew, how he doth forward his design, by astonishing the Heart with his frightful thundrings.
units.tr: 2. The other engine by which he fixes these conclusions. Though it is not argumentative, it serves to sharpen all his fallacies against the comforts of God's children. This is fear, which he sends into the mind together with his objections. That Satan can raise a storm and commotion in the heart by fear has been proved before. I shall now only show in a few points how he advances his design, by astonishing the heart with his frightful thunderings.

units.la: 1. His Objections being accompanied with Affrightments, they pass for strong undeniable Arguments, and their Fallacy is not so easily detected. Fear, as well as Anger, darkens Reason, and disables the Understanding to make a true faithful search into things, or to give a right judgment : As Darkness deceives the Senses, and makes every Bush affrightful to the Passenger ; or as muddied Waters hinder the sight : so do Fears in the Heart disable a Man to discover the silliest [?] Cheat that Satan can put upon it.
units.tr: 1. His objections come accompanied by affrightments, so they pass for strong, undeniable arguments, and their fallacy is not so easily detected. Fear, like anger, darkens reason and disables the understanding from making a true and faithful search into things, or from giving a right judgment. As darkness deceives the senses and makes every bush frightful to the traveller, or as muddied waters hinder the sight, so fears in the heart keep a man from discovering even the silliest cheat that Satan can practise upon it.

units.la: 3. These Fears make all Satan's suggestions strike the deeper, they point all his Arrows, and make them pierce (as it were) the Joynts and Marrow; they poyson and envenom them to the great increase of the Torment, and hinderance of the Cure; they bind the Objections upon them, and confirm them in a certain belief that they are all true. We have now viewed Satan's Engines and Batteries against the Servants of the Lord, for the destruction of their Joy and Peace, by Spiritual Troubles; but these are but the beginnings of sorrows, if compared with those distresses of Soul, which he sometimes brings upon them. Of which next.

Satan's method in working them, the Occasions he makes use of, the Arguments he urgeth, the strengthening of them by Fears. 3. Their Weight and Burthen explained in several Particulars.
