units.la: The last sort of Troubles by which Satan overthrows the peace of the Soul, are Spiritual Distresses; these are more grievous Agonies of Soul, under deepest apprehensions of Divine Wrath, and dreadful Fears of everlasting Damnation, differing in nature and degree, from the former sorts of Troubles; though in these Satan observes much what the same General Method, which he used in Spiritual Troubles last mentioned. For which cause, and also that these are not so common as the other, I shall speak of them with greater Brevity. Herein I shall shew, 1. Their Nature. 2. Satan's Method in working them. 3. Their Weight and Burthen.
units.tr: The last kind of trouble by which Satan overthrows the peace of the soul is spiritual distresses. These are more grievous agonies of soul, arising from the deepest apprehensions of divine wrath and dreadful fears of everlasting damnation. They differ from the former sorts of trouble in nature and degree, though in these also Satan follows much the same general method he used in the spiritual troubles mentioned last. For this reason, and because these troubles are not as common as the others, I shall treat them more briefly. Here I shall show: 1. their nature; 2. Satan's method in producing them; 3. their weight and burden.

units.la: 1. The Nature of Spiritual Distresses will be best discovered, by a consideration of those Ingredients of which they are made up, and of the different degrees thereof.
units.tr: 1. The nature of spiritual distresses will best be discovered by considering the ingredients of which they are made up, and the different degrees of them.

units.la: 2. As to the different degrees of Spiritual Distresses, we must observe: That according to the concurrence of all, or fewer of those Ingredients (for they do not always meet together, though most frequently they do) and according to the higher, or lower degrees in which these are urged upon the Conscience, or apprehended and believed by the troubled Party; these Agonies are more or less, and accordingly we may distinguish them variously. As,
units.tr: 2. As to the different degrees of spiritual distresses, we must observe that they are more or less severe according to whether all, or only some, of those ingredients concur (for they do not always meet together, though most often they do), and according to whether they are pressed upon the conscience in higher or lower degrees, and apprehended and believed by the troubled party. Accordingly we may distinguish them in various ways. For example:

units.la: Some may possibly question, Whether all extraordinary Agonies of Soul, upon the apprehension of eternal Damnation, be not the fruits of Melancholy? and if not, then what may the difference be betwixt those that proceed from Melancholy, and those that are properly the Terrours of Conscience?
units.tr: Some may perhaps question whether all extraordinary agonies of soul, arising from the apprehension of eternal damnation, are not the fruits of melancholy? And if not, then what may the difference be between those that proceed from melancholy and those that are properly the terrors of conscience?

units.la: 4. They that read the story of Spira[?], and observe his rational serious Replies, to the Discourses that were offered him for his Comfort, and his Carriage all along, will have no cause to conclude his Trouble to be only Melancholy; neither did the sober judicious By-standers ascribe his Distress to any such cause.
units.tr: 4. Those who read the story of Spira[?], and note his rational, serious replies to the discourses offered him for his comfort, and his conduct throughout, will have no reason to conclude that his trouble was only melancholy. Nor did the sober and judicious bystanders ascribe his distress to any such cause.

units.la: 5. The Agony of Christ upon the Cross, under the sense of Divine Wrath for our Sins, (though it were without Desperation) is an undeniable Proof, that there may be deep sense of God's Displeasure upon the Soul of Man; which cannot be ascribed to Melancholy.
units.tr: 5. The agony of Christ upon the cross, under the sense of divine wrath for our sins (though it was without despair), is an undeniable proof that there may be a deep sense of God's displeasure upon the soul of man, and that this cannot be ascribed to melancholy.

units.la: 2. Satan's method in procuring them: Which consists, 1. In the Occasions which he lays hold on for that end. 2. In the Arguments which he useth. 3. In the working up of their Fears, by which he confirms Men in them.
units.tr: 2. Satan's method in procuring them. It consists: 1. in the occasions he seizes on for that end; 2. in the arguments he uses; 3. in working up their fears, by which he confirms men in them.

units.la: 1. As to the Occasions: He follows much the same Course which hath been described before in Spiritual Troubles; so that I need not say much, only I shall note two things. 1. That it makes much for Satan's purpose, if the Party against whom he designs, have fallen into some grievous sins. Sins of common Magnitude, do not lay a foundation suitable to the Superstructure which he intends; he cannot plausibly argue Reprobation, or Damnation from every ordinary sin; but if he finds them guilty of something extraordinary, then he falls to work with his Accusations. The most usual sins which he takes advantage from, are (as Mr. Perkins observes) those against the Third, Sixth, and Seventh Command; sometimes those against the Ninth. Murther, Adultery, Perjury, and the wilful denial of Truth against Conscience, are the Crimes upon which he grounds his Charge, but most usually the last. Upon this the distressed Spira, and some of the Martyrs. As for the other, the more private they are, Satan hath oft the more advantage against them, because God's secret and just Judgment, will by this means bring to Light the hidden things of Darkness; and force their Consciences to accuse them, of that which no Man could lay to their Charge, that he might manifest himself to be the searcher of the Hearts, and trier of the Reins. Thus have many been forced to disclose private Murthers, secret Adulteries, and to Vomit up (though with much pain and torture) that which they have by Perjury, or Guile, extorted from others.
units.tr: 1. As to the occasions: he follows much the same course that has been described before in spiritual troubles, so I need not say much; I shall only note two things. (1) It greatly serves Satan's purpose if the person against whom he plans has fallen into some grievous sins. Sins of common magnitude do not lay a foundation suitable to the superstructure he intends; he cannot plausibly argue reprobation or damnation from every ordinary sin. But if he finds them guilty of something extraordinary, then he sets to work with his accusations. The sins he most usually takes advantage of are (as Mr. Perkins observes) those against the Third, Sixth, and Seventh commandments, and sometimes those against the Ninth. Murder, adultery, perjury, and the wilful denial of the truth against conscience are the crimes on which he founds his charge, but most usually the last. It was upon this that the distressed Spira, and some of the martyrs, were assailed. As for the other, more private sins, Satan often has the more advantage against them, because God's secret and just judgment will in this way bring to light the hidden things of darkness, and force their consciences to accuse them of what no man could lay to their charge; so that he may show himself to be the searcher of the hearts and trier of the reins. Thus many have been forced to disclose private murders and secret adulteries, and to vomit up (though with much pain and torture) what they had extorted from others by perjury or guile. (2) Where Satan does not have these particular advantages, he endeavours to prepare men for distresses by other troubles long continued.

units.la: 2. As for the Arguments which he useth, they are much-what from the same Topicks which he maketh choice of in bringing on Spiritual Troubles. Only as he aims at the Proof of a great deal more against God's Children, than that they are not Converted; so accordingly he serves up his Mediums for proof to an higher pin. His Arguments are,
units.tr: 2. As for the Arguments he uses, they are much the same topics he chooses when he brings on spiritual troubles. Only, as he aims at proving a great deal more against God's children than that they are not converted, he accordingly raises his means of proof to a higher pitch. His arguments are these:

units.la: 1. From Scriptures wrested, or misapplied. His choice of Scriptures for this purpose, is of such places as either seem to speak most sadly the dangerous and fearful Estate of Men, according to the first view and literal representation of them, through the unskilfulness of those that are to be concerned; Or of such places as do really signifie the miserable Unhappiness of some Persons, who through their own fault, have been cut off from all hope, and the possibility of the like to some others for the future. So that in framing Arguments from Scripture, the Devil useth a twofold cunning. 1. There are some Scriptures which have the word Damnation in them, applied to some particular Acts and Miscarriages of Men; when yet their intendment is not such as the word seems to sound, or as he would make them to believe. Now, when he catcheth a Child of God in such acts as are there specified, (if he finds that his Ignorance, or Timerousnes is such, as may render the Temptation feazible) he presently applies Damnation to them by the authority of those Texts. For instance, that Text of Rom. 14.23. hath been frequently abused to that end; He that doubteth, is Damned if he eat. — The word Damned there, strikes deep with a weak troubled Christian, that is not skilful in the Word of Righteousness. For whether Satan apply it to Sacramental eating (as sometimes he doth to the Ignorant, though contrary to the purpose of the Text,) or to Doubting in the general, he makes this conclusion out of it: Thou doubtest, or thou hast eaten the Sacrament doubtingly, therefore there is no hope for thee; thou art Damned. Whereas all this while, the Devil doth but play the Sophister in the abuse of the signification of words. For that Scripture evidently relates to the difference that then was in the Church, about eating those Meats that were unclean by Moses's Law : In which case the Apostle doth positively declare, that the difference betwixt clean and unclean Meats, is taken away ; so that a Christian might with all freedom imaginable, eat those Meats that were formerly unclean, with this Proviso, that he were fully perswaded in his own mind. The necessity of which satisfaction, he proves from this, That otherwise he should offend his own Conscience, which in that case must needs Condemn him (and that's the Damnation that is there spoken of); as is more evident by comparing this Verse with the next foregoing; Happy is he that Condemneth not himself. But he that doubteth, doth Condemn himself, because he eats not of Faith ; that is, from full perswasion of the lawfulnes of the thing. This Scripture then hath nothing at all in it, to the purpose for which Satan brings it ; It doth not speak of any finall sentence of Condemnation passed upon a Man for such an Act ; all, and the utmost that it saith, is only this, That it is a sin to go against the perswasion of Conscience, and consequently it puts no Man further off Salvation, than any other sin may do ; for which, upon repentance, the Sinner may be pardoned.
units.tr: 1. They come from Scriptures wrested or misapplied. His choice of Scriptures for this purpose is of two kinds: passages that seem to speak most sadly of the dangerous and fearful state of men according to the first view and literal sense of the words, through the unskilfulness of those who are concerned; or passages that really signify the miserable unhappiness of certain persons who, through their own fault, have been cut off from all hope, and the possibility of the same for others in the future. So in framing arguments from Scripture the Devil uses a twofold cunning. (1) There are some Scriptures that contain the word Damnation, applied to particular acts and failings of men, when their intended meaning is not what the word seems to sound or what he would have them believe. When he catches a child of God in such acts as are there specified (if he finds that their ignorance or timidity is such that the temptation may be made to work), he at once applies damnation to them on the authority of those texts. For instance, the text in Rom. 14.23 has often been abused to this end: He that doubteth is damned if he eat. The word damned there strikes deep into a weak, troubled Christian who is not skilled in the word of righteousness. For whether Satan applies it to sacramental eating (as he sometimes does to the ignorant, though contrary to the purpose of the text), or to doubting in general, he draws this conclusion from it: Thou doubtest, or thou hast eaten the sacrament doubtingly, therefore there is no hope for thee; thou art damned. Yet all the while the Devil only plays the sophister, abusing the meaning of words. For that Scripture evidently concerns the dispute then current in the Church about eating those meats that were unclean under Moses's law. In that case the Apostle plainly declares that the difference between clean and unclean meats is taken away, so that a Christian might with all imaginable freedom eat those meats that were formerly unclean, with this proviso, that he be fully persuaded in his own mind. The necessity of this persuasion he proves from this: otherwise he would offend his own conscience, which in that case must needs condemn him (and that is the damnation spoken of there). This is more evident by comparing this verse with the one just before it: Happy is he that condemneth not himself. But he that doubteth condemns himself, because he eats not of faith, that is, from full persuasion of the lawfulness of the thing. This Scripture, then, has nothing at all to the purpose for which Satan brings it. It does not speak of any final sentence of condemnation passed upon a man for such an act. All it says, at the utmost, is that it is a sin to go against the persuasion of conscience; consequently it puts no man further from salvation than any other sin may do, for which, upon repentance, the sinner may be pardoned.

units.la: Another Text which Satan hath frequently abused, to the very great prejudice of many, is that of 1 Cor. 11. 29. He that eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh Damnation to himself. With this Scripture he insults over the humble fearful Christian, who is sensible of his unworthiness of so great a Priviledg. Sometimes he keeps him off long from the Sacrament of the Lord's Supper, upon this very score ; That such an unworthy Wretch ought not to make such near and familiar approaches to Christ. And if at last he is perswaded to partake of this Ordinance, then (taking the advantage of the Parties Consciousnes of his great Vilenes, and the very low thoughts which he entertains of himself) he endeavours to perswade him, that now he hath destroyed himself for ever, and run upon his own irrecoverable Damnation. Thus he pleads it ; Can any thing be more plain, than that thou hast eaten and drunken unworthily? Thy own Conscience tells thee so: and can any thing be more positively asserted than this, that he that doth so, eateth and drinketh Damnation to himself? What then canst thou think of thy self, but that thou art a damned Wretch? Neither do I speak barely, what may be supposed Satan would say in this matter, but what may be proved by many Instances he hath said and urged upon the Consciences of the Weak, who have from hence concluded (to the great distress of their Souls) that by unworthy receiving of the Sacrament, they have sealed up their own Condemnation; and all this by abusing and perverting the sense of this Text. For the unworthy receiving, doth relate to the Miscarriages which he had taxed before, and it implies a careless, prophane eating; such as might plainly express the small, or unworthy esteem that they had in their Hearts for that Ordinance. And the Damnation there threatned, is not finall and irrecoverable Damnation, but Temporal Judgment; as the Apostle himself doth explain it, in the next Verses: For this cause many are sickly. — And if we would judge our selves, we should not be judged. — That is (as he further explains it) we should not be thus Chastned, or Afflicted; and the word translated Damnation, doth signifie Judgment. At the furthest, if we should take it for the Condemnation of Hell, all that is threatned would be no more than this; That such have deserved, and God in Justice might inflict the Condemnation of Hell for such an offence: Which is not only true of this sin, but of all others, which still do admit of the exception of Repentance. All this while this is nothing to the poor humbled Sinner, that judgeth himself unworthy in his most serious Examination, and greatest Diligence. Satan here plays upon the unexactness of the Translation, and the ignorance of the Party in Criticisms; for 'tis not every one that can readily answer such Captious Arguments. 2. But he hath another piece of Cunning, which is this: He doth by a singular kind of Art, threap upon Men some Scripture that really speaks of Eternal Condemnation, without any sufficient evidence in matter of Fact for the due application of them, only because they cannot prove the contrary. His proceeding herein is to this purpose: First, (After he hath prepared his way, by forming their minds to a fearful suspition of their Estate) he sets before them such Scriptures as these; God hardned the heart of Pharaoh: He hath prepared Vessels of Wrath, fitted for Destruction. Christ prayed not for the World: And that concerning the Jews, He hath blinded their eyes, and hardned their hearts, Secondly, He confidently affirms, that they are such. Thirdly, He puts them to prove the contrary, and herein he sends them to the search of God's Eternal Decrees; in which Art, Satan (like an Ignis fatuus) leads them out of the way. And though he cannot possibly determine what he affirms, he shifts off the positive proof from himself, and leaves it upon them to make out, that they are not thus determined of by God's unchangeable purpose. And because the tempted (under so great a Cloud) have no such perswasion of their present Graces, as may enable them to make sure their Election, by the Fruits of their Vocation, they are beaten off from their hold, and are brought to believe that the Argument is unanswerable: Because they cannot say they are Converted, they conclude they must be Damned; overlooking the true Answer that they might make, by keeping close to the Possibility, or Probability that they may be Converted, and so escape the Damnation of Hell. This general hope being of such high concern to the distressed, (for 'tis the first thing that must relieve them, till better Evidence come in) it is Satan's great policy to Cheat them of it, which he often doth by this Method now declared.
units.tr: Another text which Satan has often abused, to the very great harm of many, is 1 Cor. 11.29: He that eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh damnation to himself. With this Scripture he insults the humble, fearful Christian who feels his unworthiness of so great a privilege. Sometimes he keeps him long away from the Lord's Supper on this very ground: such an unworthy wretch ought not to make such near and familiar approaches to Christ. And if at last he is persuaded to partake of this ordinance, then, taking advantage of the person's consciousness of his great vileness and the very low thoughts he entertains of himself, he tries to persuade him that now he has destroyed himself for ever and run upon his own irrecoverable damnation. He pleads thus: Can anything be more plain than that thou hast eaten and drunk unworthily? Thy own conscience tells thee so. And can anything be more positively asserted than this, that he who does so eateth and drinketh damnation to himself? What then canst thou think of thyself, but that thou art a damned wretch? Nor do I speak merely of what Satan might be supposed to say in this matter, but of what can be proved by many instances in which he has said it and pressed it upon the consciences of the weak. From this they have concluded, to the great distress of their souls, that by unworthily receiving the sacrament they have sealed up their own condemnation, and all this by abusing and perverting the sense of this text. For the unworthy receiving relates to the failings which he had taxed before, and it implies a careless, profane eating, such as would plainly express the small, or unworthy, esteem that they had in their hearts for that ordinance. And the damnation there threatened is not final and irrecoverable damnation but temporal judgment, as the Apostle himself explains in the next verses: For this cause many are sickly. — And if we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged. That is (as he further explains it) we should not be thus chastened or afflicted; and the word translated damnation signifies judgment. At the very furthest, if we took it for the condemnation of hell, all that is threatened would be no more than this: such persons have deserved it, and God in justice might inflict the condemnation of hell for such an offence. This is true not only of this sin but of all others, which still admit the exception of repentance. All this is nothing to the poor humbled sinner who, in his most serious examination and greatest diligence, judges himself unworthy. Satan here plays upon the inexactness of the translation and the ignorance of the person in critical matters, for not everyone can readily answer such captious arguments.

units.la: 2. Satan doth mainly endeavour to misrepresent God to troubled Souls, and from thence he draweth out Arguments against them. In the former case of Spiritual Troubles, he misrepresents God, in that he represents only some Attributes of his, not only distinct from, but in opposition to others, by which he labours to conceal the sweet and beautiful Harmony that is among them; and also to make one Attribute, an Argument against the comfortable supporting Considerations, which another would afford. He insists upon God's Justice without respect of Mercy, upon his Holiness, without any regard of his Gracious Condescentions to the Infirmities of the Weak. But when it is his business to bring any under Spiritual Distresses, he then misrepresents God at an higher rate, and sticks not to asperse him with abominable Falshoods. There are two Lies which he commonly urgeth at this time.
units.tr: 2. Satan mainly tries to misrepresent God to troubled souls, and from this he draws arguments against them. In the earlier case of spiritual troubles, he misrepresents God by presenting only some of his attributes, not merely as distinct from the others but as in opposition to them. By this he tries to hide the sweet and beautiful harmony among them, and to turn one attribute into an argument against the comforting considerations that another would supply. He insists on God's justice without regard to his mercy, and on his holiness without any thought of his gracious condescension to the weakness of the feeble. But when his business is to plunge someone into spiritual distress, he misrepresents God at a higher rate, and does not hesitate to charge him with abominable falsehoods. There are two lies he commonly presses at this time.

units.la: 4. There is but one Argument more, that carries any probability of proof for everlasting Condemnation, and that is from an hard and impenitent Heart. How Satan will manage himself to make a Child of God believe, that he hath such an Heart; is our last observation relating to his Sophistry. And it is this, He unjustly aggravates the discomposures of the spirits of those that are troubled for Sin, and from thence draws his Arguments of irrecoverable Damnation; pleading that their Hearts are Seared, Hardned, uncapable of Repentance, and consequently of Heaven. That final Impenitency will conclude Damnation, is certain, and that some have been given up to such a judicial hardness long before Death, that they could not Repent; may not only be evidenced from the Threatning of God to that purpose, Mat. 13. Make the Heart of this People fat, &c. but also from the sad Instances of Pharaoh, (of whom 'tis said, that God hardned his Heart) and the Jews who were blinded, Rom. 11. 8. God hath given them the Spirit of slumber, Eyes that they should not see, and Ears that they should not hear. But still the Art lieth in this, How to make a Child of God believe that it's so with him. For this purpose he must take him at some advantage, he cannot terrifie him with this Argument at all times. While he is acting Repentance, with an undisturbed settled frame of Heart, 'tis not possible to make him believe he doth not, or cannot Repent; for this were to force him contrary to sense and experience. But he must take him at some season, which may, with some probability, admit of his Plea, and nothing is more proper for that design, than a troubled Heart; so that he hath in this case, two things to do.
units.tr: 4. There is only one more argument that has any appearance of proof for everlasting condemnation, and that is drawn from a hard and impenitent heart. How Satan manages to make a child of God believe that he has such a heart is our last observation on his sophistry. He unjustly magnifies the disturbances of the spirits of those who are troubled for sin, and from this he draws his arguments for irrecoverable damnation, pleading that their hearts are seared and hardened, incapable of repentance, and consequently of heaven. That final impenitence will bring damnation is certain, and that some have been given up to such a judicial hardness long before death that they could not repent may be shown not only from God's threatening to that effect, Mat. 13. Make the heart of this people fat, etc., but also from the sad examples of Pharaoh (of whom it is said that God hardened his heart) and of the Jews who were blinded, Rom. 11. 8. God hath given them the spirit of slumber, eyes that they should not see, and ears that they should not hear. But the art lies in this: how to make a child of God believe that it is so with him. For this purpose Satan must take him at some advantage, since he cannot terrify him with this argument at all times. While he is acting repentance, with a undisturbed and settled frame of heart, it is not possible to make him believe that he does not, or cannot, repent; for that would be to force him against his own sense and experience. He must therefore catch him at some season which may, with some plausibility, admit his plea, and nothing is more suited to this design than a troubled heart. So in this case he has two things to do.

units.la: 3. There is but one thing more, (besides the occasions which he takes, and the Arguments which he makes use of) relating to Satan's method for the procurement of Spiritual Distresses, and that is his endeavour to strengthen these Arguments, by the increase of fears in their Hearts.
units.tr: 3. There is one thing more to mention, besides the occasions Satan seizes and the arguments he uses, concerning his method of producing spiritual distresses: his effort to strengthen those arguments by increasing fears in their hearts.

units.la: 4. Though Fears make the Soul unactive to any thing of Comfort, because they wholly destroy its inclination, and alter its Byas to Hope; yet on the contrary, they make it very nimble, and active to pursue the conclusions of Misery, which they have helped to frame. For the spring of all the faculties of the Soul are bent that way. Hence it is, that those who are possessed with these Agonies, will eagerly plead against themselves, and with an admirable subtilty, will frame Arguments against their Peace, coin Distinctions, and make strange Evasions to escape the force of any Consolation that may be offered to them; their understandings are, as it were, whetted by their Fears to an unimaginable quickness. Who would not wonder to hear the Replies that some will give to the arguings of their Friends, that labour to comfort them? What strange answers Spira gave to those that pleaded with him? How easily he seemed to turn off the Example of Peter denying Christ, and those Scriptures that speak of God's Love to Mankind, &c. may be seen at large in his Narrative.
units.tr: 4. Though fears make the soul unable to take hold of any comfort, because they wholly destroy its inclination and turn its bias away from hope, yet on the contrary they make it very nimble and active in pursuing the conclusions of misery which they have helped to frame. For the spring of all the faculties of the soul is bent that way. Hence those possessed with these agonies will eagerly plead against themselves, and with admirable subtlety will frame arguments against their peace, coin distinctions, and make strange evasions to escape the force of any consolation offered them. Their understandings are, as it were, whetted by their fears to an unimaginable quickness. Who would not wonder to hear the replies some will give to the arguments of friends who labour to comfort them? What strange answers Spira gave to those who pleaded with him? How easily he seemed to turn aside the example of Peter denying Christ, and those Scriptures that speak of God's love to mankind, and so on, may be seen at large in his narrative.

units.la: 3. The burthen and weight of these Distresses, which how grievous, how intollerable it is, may be sufficiently seen in what hath been already said, and may be further evidenced in the Particulars following.
units.tr: 3. The burden and weight of these distresses. How grievous and intolerable it is may be sufficiently seen from what has already been said, and may be further shown in the particulars that follow.

units.la: I have presented you with Satan's Stratagems, against the Peace of God's Children: the Remedies against these and other Subtilties of our grand Enemy, I shall not offer you, because many others have done that already, to whose Writings I must refer you. Some principal Directions I have pointed at in the way, and in the General have done this for the help of the Tempted, that I have endeavoured to shew them the Methods of the Tempter, which is no small help to preserve Men from being thus imposed upon, and to recover out of his Snare those that are. 'Tis a great preservative from Sickness, and no mean advantage to the Cure, to have a discovery of the Disease, and the Causes of it. I shall conclude these Discoveries with a Caution or two.
units.tr: I have presented you with Satan's stratagems against the peace of God's children. The remedies against these and other subtleties of our grand enemy I shall not offer you, because many others have already done so, to whose writings I must refer you. I have pointed at some principal directions in the course of the work, and in general I have done this for the help of the tempted: I have endeavoured to show them the methods of the Tempter, which is no small help to preserve men from being thus imposed upon, and to recover out of his snare those who are caught. It is a great preservative from sickness, and no mean advantage to the cure, to have a discovery of the disease and its causes. I shall conclude these discoveries with a caution or two.

units.la: 2. Let none flight, or scoff at these Tremendous Judgments. 'Tis too common with Men, either to ascribe Spiritual Troubles to Melancholy, as if none were ever thus concerned, but such, as by too much serioufness in Religion, are become Mad, (a fair pretence for Carelessness) or to a whining Diffimulation: To the former I have said something before, and as for the latter, I shall only reply in the words of Spira, to one that objected Hypocrisie to him: I am a Cast-away, a Vessel of Wrath, yet dare you call it Diffembling and Frenzy, and can mock at the formidable example of the heavy Wrath of God, that should teach you Fear and Terrour? But 'tis natural to the Flesh to speak (either out of malice or ignorance) perversly of the Work of God.
units.tr: 2. Let none slight or scoff at these tremendous judgments. It is too common with men either to attribute spiritual troubles to melancholy, as if none were ever so troubled except those who, by too much seriousness in religion, have become mad (a convenient pretext for carelessness), or to a whining dissimulation. I have said something before about the former. As for the latter, I will only reply in the words of Spira, to one who charged him with hypocrisy: I am a castaway, a vessel of wrath, yet you dare to call it dissembling and frenzy, and can mock at the dreadful example of God's heavy wrath, which ought to teach you fear and terror? But it is natural to the flesh to speak perversely of the work of God, either out of malice or ignorance.
